19903-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
The American Missionary for May 1895 is volume 49, number 5. Its front matter lists auditors like Peter McCarter of Bible House, New York. The executive committee includes William Hayes Ward and Charles L. Lyman. District secretaries cover Congregational House in Boston and La Salle Street, Chicago. The American Missionary Association ran this monthly for its supporters. Names and offices fill these administrative pages.

Such lists map a national benevolent machine. The Association's schools served freedpeople across the South. Its magazine reported fields from Dakota to China. May 1895 catches the organization mid-stream, fully staffed. Researchers trace personnel through pages like these. The issue is a brick in a large archive.
22810-midnight-in-beauchamp-row-1895:
A bag stuffed with bank notes sits at the center of Midnight in Beauchamp Row, a short mystery tale dated 1895. Ned brings the money home, and his wife begs him not to leave her alone with it for the night. Their maid Tennie has gone off for a holiday, so the house stands empty except for the couple and the cash.

Fear does most of the work in the telling. Every sound in the dark house raises the stakes, and the wife's dread turns an ordinary evening into a vigil. Readers get a compact crime story built on suspense rather than gore, the kind of tale that filled magazines of the period. It rewards anyone who likes a tight plot, a house at night, and money that invites trouble.
aksakov-animisme-et-spiritisme-1895:
Alexander Aksakov sorts strange feats in two great heaps in Animisme et spiritisme, in French from 1895. Aksakov was a man of state in Russia and a chief of the field in Europe. Some feats, he says, come from the seer's own hid self: that heap is animism. The rest need the dead at work: that heap is spiritism, his true faith.

Tests and famed cases fill two fat tomes in proof. His split gave the field words it still uses each day. The book, in French, is its great sort. Few works shaped its terms so much.
arxiv-2512-00695:
Manoj Belavadi and Kathie Cameron wrote a 2025 graph theory paper on Kempe changes. A graph coloring assigns colors to points so that linked points differ. Pick two colors, and the points using them split into connected groups called Kempe chains. A Kempe swap flips the two colors inside one chain.

Swaps turn one valid coloring into another, so they map out how colorings connect. Belavadi and Cameron study graphs that avoid a fixed pattern graph, known as H-free graphs. Knowing when swaps can move between all colorings helps solve counting and sampling problems. It also bears on puzzles and timetables, where colorings model the choices.
arxiv-2512-01195:
Tao Luo, Yu Ning, and Xiande Zhang study the quantum chromatic number of certain graphs in a 2025 math paper. The chromatic number of a graph is the fewest colors needed so adjacent vertices differ. In the quantum version, players use entangled states to color cooperatively, sometimes with fewer colors than any classical method allows.

Few graph families have known quantum chromatic numbers. Orthogonality graphs are a notable exception, fully determined already. The authors study subgraphs of those graphs, and the distance-two Hamming graph, where words differing in few positions connect. Pinning down exact values shows where quantum strategies truly help.
arxiv-2512-01295:
Mihai Christodorescu and co-authors set out the safety needs for AI agents. Agents are programs that plan and act on their own. They use tools, read files, and send messages. A safe model alone does not make a safe full system.

The authors look at the whole system, not just the model. They list short-term and long-term research tasks for agent safety and privacy. Each task asks how an agent can be tricked, leak data, or cause harm. Their plan gives builders a shared map for tests, guards, and design rules that cover real use.
arxiv-2512-01495:
Joanne Lin and co-authors tackle video segmentation in dark clips. The task marks each object in each frame. Low light brings noise, blur, and low contrast. Both humans and machines find it hard. Large labeled sets for dark video are scarce too.

Fake dark clips made by past pipelines miss how real dark video degrades over time. The team's method, ELVIS, aims to lift low-light clips for better segmentation. Clearer input helps the model track objects through dark frames. Gains would aid night driving, security, and wildlife film work. The method is tested on real dark footage, not just bright clips dimmed by hand, which makes its scores harder to game.
arxiv-2512-01795:
Torrecilla Pinero and co-authors quantify risk in Voronoi service area models. Voronoi maps assign each place to its nearest service point. Straight-line distance drives that assignment. Rules like waste proximity principles rest on such maps in law.

In rough terrain or sparse infrastructure, straight lines mislead. True travel can be far longer than the map suggests. The team measures the misallocation risk that follows. Safer maps would assign services by real routes, which matters for equity in rural regions. Road-network distance is the natural fix the study points to, since travel time, not raw meters, decides who can reach a service.
arxiv-2512-01895:
Moving a facial expression from one face to another is easy within photos of real people and much harder across styles, say from a photograph to a cartoon. Avirup Dey and Vinay Namboodiri present StyleYourSmile in 2025, a method for retargeting faces across such domains without paired training examples in each style.

The hard part is keeping identity, expression, and style separate, so one can change without dragging the others along. Earlier methods often failed to generalize across domains, or needed slow test-time tuning and carefully built multi-style datasets. A method that skips those demands would make stylized animation and avatar tools far easier to build.
arxiv-2512-02095:
The Milky Way's small satellite galaxies are fossils of galaxy formation, but reading them requires separating chance variation from the physics of gas and stars. Jonah Rose and a large collaboration analyze in 2025 over a thousand simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies from the DREAMS Project.

The simulations use the TNG galaxy-formation model inside a standard cosmology, varying both the physics of ordinary matter and the cosmological settings. With so many hosts, each with its own environment and history, the team can disentangle halo-to-halo variance from the effects of baryonic feedback. The satellite populations that result give observers a sharper baseline for judging the real Milky Way.
arxiv-2512-02295:
Some spots on the Sun spout jets time and time again, like geysers. Each blast frees magnetic force stored low in the Sun's air. Aabha Monga and four co-authors probe in 2025 what drives these jets. They home in on how flows of magnetic flux meet and clash.

Flux that rises and flux that cancels out are known to feed jet birth. But what reloads one spot for blast after blast is still not clear. The team tracks how flux fields clash and build stress anew. The work feeds the broad study of how the Sun's magnetism drives blasts that can reach Earth.
arxiv-2512-02495:
Ali Mohammad-Djafari, Ning Chu, and Li Wang tackle inverse problems, where hidden causes must be inferred from indirect, noisy data. Such problems turn up across science and engineering, from medical scans to earth sensing. They are often ill posed, meaning small noise can cause large swings in the answer.

Classic fixes include regularization, which adds prior rules, and Bayesian inference, which tracks uncertainty openly. The authors combine Bayesian thinking with physics informed neural networks, which respect known physical laws. Their test case is infrared image processing, where cleaner inference could sharpen heat based pictures used in inspection and diagnosis. In plain terms, the method lets the data speak but keeps wild guesses in check.
arxiv-2512-02695:
Md Faysal Hossain and Sean B. Andersson track single tiny particles in real time as they move inside cells. Feedback driven tracking measures light from a labeled particle and steers the instrument to follow it. Watching one particle in its native setting reveals motion that snapshots cannot show.

Their double helix based method shapes the light so position can be read quickly and well. Fast, accurate estimates feed the control loop that keeps the particle centered. Better tracking opens longer, clearer views of transport and binding inside living cells, key processes in health and disease. Long clean tracks beat short bright ones when the goal is to watch a cell at work over time.
arxiv-2512-02795:
Marcus Kessel argues that code generating AI should learn from watching software run, not just reading it. Today's models train on static artifacts: source code, comments, and specifications. They rarely see recorded behavior, so they can absorb buggy or mislabeled code as if it were truth.

Deep facts about a program cannot be decided in general, so observed runs are the practical ground truth. Kessel proposes observation lakehouses: living, interactive archives of software behavior. Feeding models real execution traces could teach them what code does, not just what it looks like, cutting confident errors. Runs leave a trail that reads can check, and that trail is the part most code tools throw out too soon.
arxiv-2512-03195:
Matching job ads to skill lists is slow work by hand. Stylianos Saroglou and co-authors test language models for that task in this 2025 work. They link job vacancy texts to two European frameworks for skills and qualifications.

One framework, ESCO, lists skills, competences, and occupations. The other, EQF, sets levels for qualifications. The authors compare two methods from past work, sentence linking and entity linking. Better linking could help job seekers find fitting roles. It could also help schools see which skills employers want most. Public job services could use such links to guide training funds toward real demand.
arxiv-2512-03395:
Ratios of partition functions can reveal phase transitions. Satoshi Morita and Naoki Kawashima compute such ratios with tensor renormalization in this 2025 work. At criticality, theory predicts universal values for these dimensionless ratios.

Those values come from conformal field theory through partition functions on a torus. Tensor methods let the authors compute the ratios in practice. Matching theory and computation is a strong check on both. The approach helps study critical phenomena in magnets and other many-body systems. Universal ratios give sharp targets, because their values do not depend on material details, only on the transition class.
arxiv-2601-06695:
Sphiwe Skhosana and Weixin Yao build a sturdier mix model for grouped data in a 2026 paper. Mix models sort data into hid groups, each with its own trend line. Loose forms let those trends bend with the inputs in free ways.

Those loose forms lean on a bell shape for their noise, though. That makes their fits jumpy when wild points show up in the data. Thick tails in the noise also break their care in real use. Their fix adds a tainted bell part that soaks up wild points. The loose parts keep the bend that made mix models prized at first. The mix thus bends without breaking when data turn rough or wild. The model suits grouped data where extremes are the norm, not the rare case.
arxiv-2601-06895:
A 2026 arXiv paper in pure math gives exact values for a class of Euler sums. Euler sums are sums built from harmonic numbers, which add up the parts one over one, one over two, and so on. Here the sums also use parts with fractions, not whole steps alone. The paper treats two such sums side by side.

In one sum, each term pairs a harmonic number with a power term. In the next, the signs of the terms switch from plus to minus as the sum goes on. Three whole-number inputs steer both sums. One input must not equal one. For readers in number theory, the paper gives closed forms where past work had sums with no short form. Such forms let readers check and reuse the sums with care.
arxiv-2601-07095:
Research by Tadashi Wadayama and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with Score-Based VAMP with Fisher-Information-Based onsager correction. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors propose score-based VAMP (SC-VAMP). A variant of vector approximate message passing (VAMP) in which the Onsager correction is expressed and computed via conditional Fisher information. Thereby enabling a Jacobian-free implementation.

Using learned score functions, SC-VAMP constructs nonlinear minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimators through Tweedie’s formula and derives. The corresponding Onsager terms from the score-norm statistics. Avoiding the need for analytical derivatives of the prior or likelihood. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07495:
L. I. Danilov studies the spectrum of a charged particle in a magnetic field, in this 2026 mathematics and physics preprint. The model is the Landau Hamiltonian with an added periodic electric potential. Landau Hamiltonians describe electrons moving under a steady magnetic field. Their energy levels are a classic subject in quantum mechanics.

Danilov proves that, for every natural number m, special periodic potentials exist with certain spectral behavior. The potentials he constructs are smooth, nonconstant, and have zero mean value. They depend analytically on a small parameter. The result concerns what happens near a chosen Landau level. Readers in mathematical physics get a precise statement about how a periodic electric field can reshape magnetic energy levels.
arxiv-2601-07595:
A large IceCube and gravitational wave collaboration searches for cosmic events that emit both neutrinos and gravitational waves. Joint sources have been a primary target for LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA, and IceCube. Finding one would reveal processes that neither signal shows alone. The search uses data from the third observing run of LIGO and Virgo. Their 2026 preprint describes a deep search of that data.

High-energy neutrinos point back to violent cosmic accelerators. Gravitational waves reveal mergers and collapses of compact objects. A joint detection could connect the two pictures for the same event. The authors note targets from compact object mergers to relativistic outflows. Even a careful non-detection sets useful limits. Multi-messenger astronomers use such searches to plan the next observing runs.
arxiv-2601-07695:
A 2026 preprint tackles a weak point of vision-language models: giving exact numbers for three-dimensional scenes. Precise numerical prediction is a bottleneck for 3D scene understanding. Traditional reinforcement learning for this task ranks answers against each other. That relative approach often suffers sparse rewards and unstable gradients. It also fails to use the checkable signals that 3D physical constraints provide.

The authors propose a smooth verifiable reward, presented under the name Smooth Operator. Verifiable rewards pay the model only when an answer can be checked as right. Smoothing that signal aims to keep training stable while staying honest. Better spatial numbers would help robots and assistants judge distance, size, and position. The paper targets scholars training vision-language models for grounded spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2601-07995:
Laurits Lyngbaek and coauthors ask whether the shape of sentiment in language models curves like a banana. Work in the humanities often needs sentiment scores set in context, on a smooth scale. Concept vector projections treat sentiment as a direction in embedding space. They give smooth scores in more than one language that match human judgments with care. How well the method moves to new fields, and what it takes for granted, are still not well probed. Their 2026 preprint probes both points.

If that direction bends, a straight line read will misread texts at the far ends. Testing the shape tests the method's foundations. How well it moves decides whether scholars can trust scores on new kinds of text. The authors span computational linguistics and digital humanities groups in Denmark. The paper serves scholars who apply sentiment tools to cultural material. It checks the ruler before measuring with it.
arxiv-2601-08295:
Gregor Autischer, Kerstin Waxnegger, and Dominik Kowald test self-certification for high-risk AI systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper takes facial emotion recognition as the working example. The European Union AI Act sets broad duties for high-risk systems, but harmonized standards remain incomplete.

The team applies the Fraunhofer AI assessment catalogue as a certification framework. They run a complete self-certification cycle on the emotion recognition system. That full pass shows where catalogue checks work in practice and where gaps stay open. For compliance teams, the study offers a concrete rehearsal of duties that will soon be enforced across Europe.
arxiv-2601-08495: A. Conta and four co-authors present a toolchain for shuttling trapped-ion qubits in segmented traps. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that scalable trapped-ion computing needs fast, reliable ion transport. Ions must move through complex segmented radiofrequency trap architectures without excess motional excitation. Extra motion heats the ions and degrades gate quality. The toolchain generates time-dependent electrode voltages for fast, low-excitation shuttling in a systematic way. Reliable shuttling is a building block for larger trapped-ion processors with many zones.
arxiv-2601-09095:
Yin-Fa Shen and four co-authors plan a hunt for heavy neutrinos at the Large Hadron Collider. A neutrino is a near ghost bit that skims through stuff. A heavy form could solve open asks on why plain neutrinos weigh so slight. Past hunts rest on plain links of the heavy form to known bits. This team lets those links vary by bit type.

They add a new make path at the lab and sharp learn tools to pick its trace. The trace is a charged bit, lost push, and two jets of spray. A reader in core physics gets a hunt that can reach zones past hunts left blind.
arxiv-2601-09395:
Ricardo Mamede, José Luis Santos, and Diogo Soares count special spellings of permutations. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies reduced words, the shortest ways to write a permutation as a product of simple swaps. A commutation class groups spellings that differ only by swapping distant, commuting swaps.

The authors bound the number of one-element commutation classes, classes whose spelling admits no commutation at all. From that bound they prove a conjecture linking the number of reduced words to the number of commutation classes. Counts like these sit at the heart of Coxeter group theory and Schubert calculus. The result tightens what is known about how permutations can be spelled.
arxiv-2601-09695:
Michael Konstantinou, Renzo Degiovanni, and Mike Papadakis check whether newer language models write better unit tests. Their 2026 arXiv paper revisits LLM-based test generation as models evolve. Automated test generation is a growing use of language models in software engineering.

Used alone, models produce many tests that fail to compile or cover little code. The authors ask how much newer model versions improve that record. The answer tells teams whether to upgrade models, add post-processing, or both. Test generation only saves effort if the tests run and actually exercise the code.
arxiv-2601-09795:
Lucas Michel builds counterexamples in a theory used to carve space into simple cells. His 2026 arXiv paper constructs exotic cylindrical algebraic decompositions and cells. Such decompositions, enriched with topological properties, serve logic, algorithm design, and robot motion planning.

They also help study the topology of semi-algebraic sets. Michel gives explicit examples that refute several conjectures and open questions of J. H. Davenport and others. Counterexamples prune false hopes from the map of a theory like this one. They show exactly which nice properties a decomposition of this kind cannot always have in practice.
arxiv-2601-09895:
Connor Quinn proves bounds for a wave flow on a square torus. The flow tracks how a wave spreads in time and space. Bounds of Strichartz type say how much the wave can pile up. Quinn works at the key power where such bounds are most hard to get.

He shows the bound holds with no loss. The wave starts with its tones in a fixed band. The time span is short, and its length rests on the tone size. Sharp bounds with no loss are prized in wave work. On closed spaces, some loss is the norm, so a clean bound stands out.
arxiv-2601-09995:
Masahito Hayashi and Jinpei Zhao bring a classic tool into quantum work. In classic stats, a chain of linked vars can split in two ways at once. This trait is named double Markovity. It backs proofs that Gauss forms are best for some tasks.

The pair prove a quantum form of the trait. They work with states split in three parts. Two chain forms can hold at once. When they do, set tests on two parts yield one shared label. That label splits the first part from the pair. The result opens a path to quantum forms of those best form proofs.
arxiv-2601-10095:
Yuda Li, Shaoyuan Li, and Xiang Yin work out which states can reach a goal in a timed net. Such nets model lines where steps must sync and waits stack. They are named max plus linear systems. The math tracks the worst link in a chain.

The team looks back in time. They seek all states that can hit a goal set in a set count of steps. They use shape tools named polyhedra to mark those states. Sharp marks of this kind help plan lines and check them. They show if a line can meet a due time from a given start.
arxiv-2601-10695:
Sriram Ganeshan and Alan T. Dorsey bring quantum geometry to a classic model of the air and sea. The rotating shallow water equations drive much of weather and ocean modeling. Their waves also mirror waves in electron gases and active fluids. Recent work stressed the topology of these wave bands, their global twists.

The authors build the complementary view, computing the full quantum geometric tensor for the linearized model on a rotating plane. That tensor captures how wave states change shape across the band. It can reveal forces and drifts that topology alone misses. The work links geophysical flows to ideas from modern condensed matter physics.
arxiv-2601-10795:
A Euclid Collaboration paper takes up weak lensing, the slight bending of galaxy images by gravity. Surveys that use lensing must correct for the point spread function, the blur of the telescope itself. For a space telescope, that blur is diffraction-limited. The correction depends on each galaxy's spectral energy distribution, its color profile across wavelengths.

So every galaxy in the survey needs a well-known spectrum before its shape can be trusted. The paper works through that requirement for Euclid. Small shape errors, summed over millions of galaxies, could fake or hide dark matter signals. The study is part of the careful groundwork that makes lensing maps believable.
arxiv-2601-10895:
Chunhui Liu bounds the rational points that conics can supply on a cubic surface. A cubic surface is a shape cut out by a degree-three equation. Its rational points, solutions with whole-number ratios, are a classic topic in number theory. Conics lying on the surface can carry many such points, so counting them needs care.

Liu gives a uniform upper bound on the rational points of bounded height that these conics provide. The proof generalizes Salberger's global determinant method through Arakelov geometry. Uniform bounds matter because they hold across families, not just for one surface. The result feeds the long effort to say how many rational points a shape can hold.
arxiv-2601-11195:
Jiaming Huang and Luca Neri work on a core task in applied economics here. Their 2026 preprint deals with SVAR models, used to trace shocks. A key step is to name the shocks with proxy variables. In real work, teams face a zoo of such proxies to pick from.

Most past frames ask for exact exogeneity from the proxy. That is, the proxy must link to one shock and no others. Huang and Neri drop that strict demand in their frame. They use ranking bounds on how proxies link to shocks. A smooth quality score sets how much slack each proxy gets. The frame aims at claims that hold up when proxies are flawed.
arxiv-2601-11295:
Kareem Abdelmaqsoud and four coauthors design tungsten alloys on a computer. Their 2026 preprint seeks alloys that bend rather than snap. Tungsten stands heat and radiation better than most metals. That makes it a top pick for harsh spots like fusion reactors.

The flaw of tungsten is that it is brittle by nature. It is also hard to print with additive methods. Printing gives free shapes and fast prototype runs for parts. A ductile, printable tungsten alloy would unlock those gains. The team's design work is done in silico, by computation. It hunts mixes that keep the strengths and lose the brittleness.
arxiv-2601-11395:
Alberto Dominguez Corella and Onesimo Hernandez-Lerma prove a maximum principle for control. Their 2026 preprint covers discrete-time systems and dynamic games. Optimal control in discrete time steps drives many models. The systems here are deterministic and can shift over time.

The team treats both finite and infinite time horizons. With Gateaux differentials, they prove a discrete maximum principle. It stands next to the known continuous-time version. A transversality condition joins it as a needed condition. The pair is necessary for any optimal control path. Under extra assumptions, the pair is also sufficient. The team then applies the result to dynamic games. Games add rivals whose moves shape each player's best plan.
arxiv-2601-11495:
Hlel Missaoui proves global regularity for Musielak-Orlicz equations in this work. The 2026 preprint deals with elliptic equations in divergence form. Solutions gain C1-alpha regularity across the whole domain here. That means gradients exist and vary in a controlled way.

The equations have Musielak-Orlicz growth, a flexible general form. Boundary conditions can be Dirichlet or Neumann in the results. Bounded generalized solutions are the class covered by the work. The findings extend several known regularity results at once. Special cases include variable exponent spaces, a hot topic. Orlicz spaces and mixed p-q growth cases also fall out. One theorem thus covers many growth laws used in practice.
arxiv-2601-11895:
Pareesa Ameneh Golnari, Adarsh Kumarappan, Wen Wen, and their co-authors built a code test set from real developer data. The set, DevBench, holds 1,800 tasks in six code tongues and six task kinds. The tasks come from real telemetry, such as API use and code purpose.

Most code tests use toy tasks cut off from real work. A set drawn from real use can grade models on what devs truly do. It can also show which task kinds still trip models up. The work gives a shared scale for code models in real settings.
arxiv-2601-11995:
Donghuo Zeng, Hao Niu, Yanan Wang, and Masato Taya learn joint traits for sound and image clips. Clips that truly match should sit close in the trait space. Chance pairs, such as background noise or off-screen events, should not.

Most past tools use sparse labels and treat each joint clip as a true match. That bakes in noise. The team infer a latent graph of links between sound and image parts. A graph-led trait could be more clean for search and tagging of video.  Cleaner traits should lift search and tag scores for clips.
arxiv-2601-12195:
Nathaniel Gallup and Leo Gray prove a ring tied to intervals in the Bruhat order is Cohen-Macaulay. The group is the infinite symmetric group, all bijections of the whole numbers. Its Bruhat order sorts group terms by a known rule.

They study the order complex of set intervals in that order. Its Stanley-Reisner ring is non-Noetherian, so the claim needs a form for ideals and weak unmixedness. Cohen-Macaulay rings have tidy depth traits. The result links combinatorics of the infinite group to algebra.  The ring is built from the order complex of the intervals.
arxiv-2601-12695:
Hiroshi Okajima, Shun Shirahama, Tatsunori Hayashi, and Nobutomo Matsunaga work on system identification under noise. Model based control needs accurate mathematical models to guarantee performance and stability. Process and sensor noise make such models hard to obtain in practice. The team propose an algorithm that derives polytopic uncertainty models instead of one fixed model.

Their idea treats noise induced parameter swings as intrinsic uncertainty. A polytope then bounds the set of models that fit the data. The construction is systematic and uses a cyclic reformulation, per the title. A bounded set of models lets control design plan for the worst case inside it. That yields safer controllers for noisy real plants.
arxiv-2601-12895:
Chan Naseeb and five co authors build a deep learning system to guard identity documents. Generative AI models have escalated the threat of synthetic manipulation of ID documents. Face swapping and text inpainting attacks can fake a document with care. A fake that passes visual checks threatens banks, borders, and online verification.

Their architecture is called TwoHead-SwinFPN. It performs binary classification and precise localization of manipulated regions at the same time. Two heads share one backbone, so detection and localization inform each other. Knowing where a forgery sits helps human reviewers trust the verdict. Unified systems like this could harden document checks against AI era fraud.
arxiv-2601-13295:
Arpandeep Khatua and co-authors test if AI coding agents can act as teammates yet. To fix a team clash takes more than task skill. It takes social sense, the skill to find shared ground and build a deal all can take. As agents do more joint work, they need that same sense.

The team built a bench called CooperBench to test it. They start from a claim that today's agents lack such skills. Agents may each do fine solo work yet fail to mesh. The bench puts them in joint code tasks where they must sort clashes to pass. For agent builders, the gap it shows is a to do list, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-13395:
Andrew Zheng and Adam R. Stinchcombe grow the adjoint method to costs that are not holomorphic. The adjoint method is a fast way to get gradients in opt tasks with binds. It was built for real valued tasks whose parts split in the standard way. With complex values, as in radio and signal work, costs can fail that split.

Such costs are called non holomorphic. They are not differentiable in the standard sense. The pair give a broad adjoint form that can still yield gradients for them. That opens fast opt to a class of inverse tasks in electromagnetics and signal work that the old form could not serve.
arxiv-2601-13495:
J. Ferrer Asensio and co-authors track a small ring molecule and its heavy twins toward cold cores in the Perseus cloud. In such cores, cold and freeze out of carbon monoxide make heavy swaps fast. The molecule is cyclopropenylidene, a three carbon ring made early in chem growth. Its heavy forms tag gas phase heavy swap in such zones.

The cores span prestellar cores, on the edge of star birth, and starless cores with no star yet. By read of the ring and its twins in both kinds, the team can set how far heavy swap has run. That stage marks the clock of a core on its way to a star.
arxiv-2601-14095:
Babak Miraftab, Pat Morin, and Yelena Yuditsky link two measures of graph complexity in 2026. The basis number of a graph counts how edge cycles can be based on few sets. Pathwidth measures how close a graph is to a simple path in structure. The team proves two results relating the basis number to path decompositions.

Their first result shows the basis number is at most four times the pathwidth. A bound like this lets one measure stand in for an other. Graph measures guide algorithm design for networks, maps, and circuits. Firm links between them simplify many proofs.
arxiv-2601-14195:
Frederik Glitzner and David Manlove study matchings that are almost stable, from a minimax angle in 2026. Stability is crucial in matching markets, from hospital residency allocations to roommate assignments. In many real settings, full stability is impossible to achieve. Or it can come at the cost of leaving many agents unmatched.

Almost-stable matchings relax the stability demand in a controlled way. A minimax view minimizes the worst instability any agent faces. A preliminary version appears at AAMAS 2026. Better near-stable rules could fill more posts while keeping disputes low.
arxiv-2601-14395:
Daxal H. Mehta, John A. Regan, and Lewis Prole study the growth of light seed black holes in this 2026 paper. Light seeds form at the end point of the first generation of Population III stars. Those were the first stars in the early universe. The seeds appear as early as redshift 30 to 40, in low-mass dark matter halos.

The open question is how such small seeds grow. To become the giants seen later, they must gain mass fast in a young, harsh setting. The paper follows that growth problem. Readers get a study of one seed path for early black holes, set against the tight time the early universe allows.
arxiv-2601-14595:
Qiyue Mei and Michael Fu build a security analyzer for cloud scripts in this 2026 paper. Infrastructure as Code lets teams provision large-scale cloud and on-premise environments automatically. It cuts repetitive manual setup. The automation is a double-edged sword, though. A single misconfiguration in an IaC script can propagate widely, leading to severe downtime and security risks.

Their tool, IntelliSA, is an intelligent static analyzer for IaC security smell detection. A security smell is a pattern that hints at a flaw, even if it is not yet an exploit. The analyzer combines symbolic rules with neural inference. The read is plain. It shows how one bad line in a script can open a hole in a whole cloud. Readers get a checker that reads deployment scripts the way auditors wish they could.
arxiv-2601-14895:
Xinyi Zheng, Yunze Liu, and a team of co-authors build a memory system for machines that move through space. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents SpatialMem. The system stores a scene as one single record that a machine can search.

The record joins three kinds of data. It holds the 3D shape of a place, the meaning of what is in it, and words that name those things. Metric anchoring ties the record to true measured positions. Fast retrieval lets the system pull stored facts back at speed whenever a query asks for them.
arxiv-2601-14995:
Mojuan Yin, Ruohui Wang, Rui Zhou, Xueguang Qiao, and Shougang Zhang build a new way to sense tiny shaking through optical fiber. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with fiber-optic vibration sensors. Such sensors are weak at very low frequencies, the slow end of shaking.

The team uses an optical lattice clock, tuned by a method called Floquet engineering. Shaking in the wound fiber shifts the light's phase. The clock's tuned spectra read that shift out. The goal is to keep the sensor sharp from 200 hertz all the way down to near zero.
arxiv-2601-15095:
Biman Bagchi studies how stiff chain molecules fold up in a poor solvent. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with semiflexible polymers. In a poor solvent the chains collapse, and they can form globules, toroids, or rodlike bundles.

Two forces compete to shape the result. Attractive forces pull the chain inward, while stiffness resists bending. Simulations and experiments on stiff and conjugated polymers show complex crossovers between shapes. What is still missing is one single unified theory of those shape changes. Bagchi works steadily toward that missing unified account of the crossovers.
arxiv-2601-15195:
Ramtin Ehsani, Sakshi Pathak, and co-authors study what happens when AI coding agents submit work to real projects. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with pull requests on GitHub. Agents now act as contributors in their own right, not just as helpers at a human's side.

Agentic contributions are rising fast across real repositories. Yet many of these pull requests fail to be merged, and little is known about why. The authors run an empirical study of the failed ones. They sort the failure modes so builders can see where agents go wrong.
arxiv-2601-15295:
Yi Wang, John Joon Young Chung, and co-authors build a tool for writing interactive stories with AI. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with interactive narrative. Authors craft a space of possible story paths, and the player's input picks which path becomes real.

Generative AI can improvise fresh content inside that space as the player acts. The authors present Elsewise, an authoring tool for this kind of work. It shows the possibility space as a visual map. Writers can see the branches their story offers and where the AI may take them.
arxiv-2601-15395:
Tamunotonye Harry, Ivoline Ngong, and co-authors argue that a user's momentary state beats their fixed traits. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how people interact with language models. Interactions vary with who the user is, and with the context of the moment.

Existing persona datasets capture only the fixed traits. They ignore state, the pressure of the situation at hand. The authors introduce Chameleon, a dataset of contextual psychological profiles. It covers thousands of profiles from Reddit users, each measured across multiple contexts, so the role of state can finally be studied.
arxiv-2601-15795:
Erick Gushiken and Tetsuo Hyodo study near-threshold states in hadron physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Near a threshold, a bound state can turn into a resonance. Mass scaling describes how its mass moves during that change. Decay channels complicate the picture. The authors ask how decay affects the scaling. They use potential models to isolate the effect.

One model varies the strength of a square-well potential. It traces the pole trajectory as a bound state becomes a resonance. Decay enters in two ways. A single-channel complex potential handles it simply. A coupled-channel real potential handles it in more detail. Comparing the two shows which effects are real and which are model artifacts. Such care matters for reading exotic hadron signals.
arxiv-2601-15895:
Anne Arzberger, Enrico Liscio, and co-authors reframe AI alignment as a shared practice in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI systems now sit inside everyday work. Value misalignment has become a pressing concern. Mainstream alignment work stays model-centric, they argue. It treats users as passive recipients of preset values. Users are better seen as epistemic agents. They meet misalignment during real interactions and respond to it.

The authors draw on situated perspectives. Alignment, in their view, is co-constructed in human-AI interaction. The title names their participatory approach to situating AI values. That means values get worked out where systems are used, with the people affected. For design teams, the shift is practical: build ways for users to surface and negotiate value conflicts.
arxiv-2601-16395:
Sánchez-Salcedo sums the wake of a mass that moves through a flat gas layer. His 2026 preprint deals with the Bondi Hoyle Lyttleton flow. That flow is the wake left by a mass in a gas stream. Here the gas sits in a layer with a set height scale. The mass sits in the mid plane of that layer.

He works the mass and speed forms along the wake tail. A one dim model keeps the sums clear and fast. Wake forms tell how much gas the mass can pull in. They also show how layer height bends the wake shape. The work aids sums of star and hole feeds in disks.
arxiv-2601-16595:
Dafne Zorzetto and coauthors set Bayes tools for diet cause sums on rich data. Their 2026 preprint deals with how diet drives health in folk. Diet facts are rich, with many foods tied as one. Cause sums on such data are hard to make firm. The team uses a factor map to cut diet to key forms.

Non parametric Bayes tools then weigh cause acts of those forms. Firm cause marks guide health rules and lone diet plans. Bad sums could push wrong rules to wide use. The work seeks cause tools that own their doubt. It serves health teams who read big diet sets.
arxiv-2601-16695:
A. C. Cem Say probes where quantum machines beat plain ones by a hair. Space is the scarce good in his tests, not time. Below a small space cap, quantum tools are known to win. Past that cap, just one win was known. His 2026 preprint sharpens that edge with finer tools.

The space caps here grow slower than log of log of input size. At those caps, quantum steps can solve tasks plain steps can't. Say's math keeps the gap true for crisp time bounds too. Such fine wins map the true edge of quantum power. They guide where small quantum gear may first pay off.
arxiv-2601-16795:
Kenan Begovic, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, and Qutaibah Malluhi guard Linux PCs from ransomware. Such crime code locks files by scrambling them. The scrambling is the crime's core act. Blocks must catch bad scrambling but let good use pass. Their 2026 preprint builds a guard that weighs risk in real time.

Their guard pairs smart learning with firm access rules. Each file act gets a risk score as it starts. High-risk acts get blocked before harm spreads. Low-risk acts flow on with no fuss. Guards like this could save firms from lock-out extortion.
arxiv-2601-16895:
Nakul Poudel, Richard Simon, and Cristian Linte test sight-and-text AI for surgery help. Surgery is a hard craft with fast, high-stakes calls. AI could back those calls with live guidance. Most surgery AI sees in one mode, sight or text. That lone view caps its grasp of the work flow. Their 2026 preprint grades big sight-text models on tool spotting.

Tool spotting marks each tool in the surgery view. The team checks how well the big models do it. Sound grades show if such models are fit for the room. They also show where lone-mode tools still win. Safe help in surgery needs proof of this sort.
arxiv-2601-17595:
Christian Sarmiento-Cano and co-authors repurpose water Cherenkov detectors for farm soil moisture. These detectors were built to catch cosmic rays. The team uses cosmic-ray neutron sensing to read soil water. Their approach beats standard neutron probes in key ways. It senses low moisture well. It also covers larger soil volumes with no need to dig probes in.

High-resolution moisture maps guide irrigation with care. Water savings matter in dry farm zones. A no-dig sensor can watch fields for long spans. Cosmic-ray methods turn a physics tool into a farm tool. The work tests that cross-field move in practice. It could widen precision agriculture's reach.
arxiv-2601-17895:
Bin Tan and a large team of co-authors teach machines to sense depth by hiding it. Their 2026 preprint presents masked depth modeling for spatial perception. Tasks like self-driving and robot handling need a firm grasp of 3D space. A model that can guess depth in a scene is a core part of that grasp. The authors train models by masking depth data and asking them to fill the gaps.

Learning to fill gaps forces a model to use the shape cues in a scene. Edges, sizes, and layout all hint at how far things are. That skill should transfer to new scenes and new tasks. The work sits in the push for vision systems that read the physical world well enough to act in it safely.
arxiv-2601-18095:
Anirban Polley simulates how alcohols of different lengths settle into cell-like membranes. His 2026 preprint uses atomistic molecular dynamics. The molecules are 1-alkanols, used as anesthetics and as agents that act on membranes. Their effect shows a cutoff: past a chain length, added length stops adding effect. The molecular basis of that cutoff is still unclear. Polley runs extensive simulations of the molecules entering a raft-like lipid bilayer.

The bilayer mixes lipids the way cell membrane rafts do. Watching where each chain length prefers to sit can explain the cutoff. Such insight links chemistry to how anesthesia works at the membrane level. It may also guide the design of membrane-active drugs.
arxiv-2601-18195:
Linhan Cao and co-authors use retrieval to teach machines to judge video quality in words. Their 2026 preprint presents QualiRAG. Quality assessment is moving past a single score toward accounts that a person can read and check. That shift demands fine perception in space and time, plus outside context. Current methods lean on fine-tuning or reinforcement learning over hand-built instruction sets, which cost heavy labeling and adapt poorly.

Retrieval-augmented generation offers another path. The system can fetch context that supports its quality judgments. Richer, grounded accounts help streaming services and camera makers alike. The work aims for quality tools that explain themselves.
arxiv-2601-18395:
Mikel Zubillaga and three colleagues study how to pull facts out of whole files with the help of large language models. The task asks a model to fill a fixed form with the names and links named in the text. Most teams tell the model to give one safe reply, the same each time, to keep the output calm.

The team shows that this safe habit wastes a real chance. When the model is let to try more than once, its tries vary, and some tries are much better than the safe one. A smart pick among the tries can thus beat the one-shot path. That holds most of all for models that think step by step. The lesson is plain: do not be greedy, but sample first and then choose with care.
arxiv-2601-18495:
F. J. Polanco-Rodríguez, C. Krafft, and P. Savoini report a first sight of a wave change in the wind that streams from the Sun. Waves in that thin gas can feed on each other and spawn new waves. A craft near the Sun caught a burst of radio waves from a fast stream of electrons. Its fine kit let the team read the field with great care.

In that burst they saw one kind of wave split into a new wave that can fly free. The split had been set out in maths but not seen in the Sun's wind till now. The find shows that fine kit can catch faint steps in how waves trade push. It also gives a check for the maths of thin gas waves. Such steps shape how the Sun's wind heats and how its bursts reach Earth.
arxiv-2601-18595:
Joseph Cotnareanu and three colleagues blend two ways of thought to solve hard sense tasks. The tasks ask for the best cause of a set of facts, a kind of backwards thought. Language models are strong at plain logic steps but weak at plans that need long proof paths. A split fix turns the task into strict logic and hands it to a solver built for that work.

That split can work, but it can also lose the soft sense that the task needs. Their blend keeps both sides in play, so soft sense and strict proof check each other. A fair blend could give replies that are both apt and sound. It may serve law, health, and fault hunts, where a cause must be both likely and proved step by step. The work maps how to strike that blend.
arxiv-2601-18695:
Christian Hirsch, Moritz Otto, and Anne Marie Svane study how points spread by a rule of push and pull act in the large. Each point in their sets is placed by a joint rule: points may shun each other or draw near, by a pair cost. Such sets model atoms, trees, and cells in which each thing's place leans on its mates. The team ask what the sums over such sets do as the view grows wide.

They show two things. First, a thinned form of the set acts close to a pure chance set with no links at all. Next, sums of shape traits of the set swing by the famed bell rule as the view grows. Their work takes in sets whose pull can reach with no cap. It also takes in points that bear marks. Firm rules back their use.
arxiv-2601-18795:
Amrith Setlur and four colleagues find a way to reuse old work when training thought tools on hard tasks. On a hard task, a tool's own tries are most all wrong. With no right try in hand, the learn step has no push and stalls. But old tries sit in store from past runs, some made by past forms of the tool or by pro hands. Those old tries hold right starts that the tool would take a long time to find a-new.

Their plan starts the tool's new tries from the tails of those old ones. The tool must still solve the last steps in its own style, so it learns. Old work, in the form of past chip time, is thus spent twice. A thrift of that kind could cut the cost of thought training a lot.
arxiv-2601-19395:
Saeed Nasehi, Farhana Choudhury, and Egemen Tanin bring transformer models to the messy routing problems of real streets. Real world vehicle routing must handle delivery time windows, refuel or recharge stops, and travel costs that differ by direction. Neural methods shine on clean textbook versions but struggle with that mess.

Their model, SEAFormer, is aware of spatial proximity and edges, the facts of the road network itself. Grounding the model in the map's structure should help it respect real constraints. Routing sits under delivery, repair fleets, and transit, so gains here save fuel and hours at scale.
arxiv-2601-19495:
Daniel Gillies, Andrea Banfi, and Adam Martin work in particle theory, where new physics is often described with a tool called an effective field theory. Such a theory works only below a set energy scale. Past that scale, its predictions stop being trustworthy. The team tests a fix called clipping, used in computer simulations of particle collisions.

Clipping throws out any simulated event where a pair of W bosons is too heavy. The cut keeps the pair below the new physics scale, where the theory should still hold. The authors check whether this trick really keeps the simulation valid. Their test focuses on the high-energy tails of the data, where the theory is most likely to break down. The work helps collider studies set honest limits on new physics.
arxiv-2601-19595:
Jiří Němeček and four colleagues work on fairness in artificial intelligence. AI systems now help decide loans, care, and other high-stakes outcomes. Laws such as the European Union's AI Act demand that bias be reduced. Yet the law is vague about what counts as bias, leaving builders to fill the gap.

The authors focus on intersectional fairness, where harm can hide in combined groups, such as older women or young migrants. They use mixed-integer optimization, a exact solving method, to build models that meet fairness goals. Their approach aims to be transparent as well as fair. Clear rules matter when a decision must be explained to the person it affects. The work offers one concrete path through a vague legal demand.
arxiv-2601-19695:
Matteo Greco, writing for the ATLAS Collaboration, reviews the hunt for supersymmetry at the Large Hadron Collider. Supersymmetry proposes a partner particle for every known particle. It would solve several open problems in the Standard Model at once. Arguments from naturalness suggest the partners of gluons and of third-generation quarks should be light enough to produce at the collider.

The review covers searches for the strong production of these particles with the ATLAS detector. Strong production means the new particles are made through the strong nuclear force, giving the highest rates. No discovery is claimed; instead the searches map where the particles are not. Each null result trims the space of viable theories. The summary guides future searches at higher energy.
arxiv-2601-19795:
Deeksha Arun, Kevin W. Bowyer, and Patrick Flynn study a nuisance for ear-based biometrics: accessories. Earrings and earphones partly cover the ear in photos. That occlusion hurts recognition systems, especially in uncontrolled settings. The authors test whether image inpainting can repair the damage before recognition runs.

Their method uses a diffusion model, trained to fill in missing image regions. It is accessory-aware, targeting the kinds of occlusion accessories cause. The repaired images are then fed to transformer-based ear recognition systems. If inpainting restores performance, systems could accept more real-world photos. The study measures how much of the loss this preprocessing can win back. The test is plain and fair.
arxiv-2601-20195:
Chaoqun Du, Zhiyu Cao, and Zhonghuai Hou study how to steer the self-assembly of active colloids, tiny particles that move on their own. Self-assembly out of equilibrium can build materials with chosen patterns from the bottom up. The hard part is guiding the process toward one target structure instead of many possible ones.

The authors propose a dissipation bias principle for targeted assembly. The idea is that controlling how energy is dissipated changes how often local parts rearrange, and how strongly. By tuning that tendency, builders may coax particles into the pattern they want. The principle could guide work on smart materials and micro-scale devices.
arxiv-2601-20495:
Smaranika Banerjee and three colleagues predict the ultraviolet light from kilonovae when a neutron star merger's jet strikes its own ejecta. A kilonova glows after two neutron stars collide and spray out heavy elements. The authors study the first day of that glow, when the jet plowing into the debris should leave a signature.

They use detailed atomic opacities suited to the first hours after merger. They vary jet power and opening angle to see how the signal changes. Early ultraviolet data could reveal whether a jet formed at all, a key fact about how these mergers launch their beams.
arxiv-2601-20595:
Xinwei Qiang and four colleagues present AutoOverlap, a way to overlap computation and communication more finely in large GPU workloads. Communication has become a first-order bottleneck at scale. Existing distributed compilers overlap whole compute and communication kernels at the stream level, a coarse approach.

That coarseness costs extra kernel launches, forces device-wide synchronization at kernel boundaries, and leaves slack when the slowest piece stretches the communication tail. AutoOverlap schedules in chunks for finer overlap. Shaving this overhead matters for training runs that span thousands of chips. The win shows up as less dead time on chips that cost a great deal per hour of use.
arxiv-2601-20695:
Denitsa Baykusheva and a large team of co-authors study how light can steer quantum matter. Their 2026 paper centers on Hubbard excitons. An exciton is a bound pair formed inside a material after light hits it. The Hubbard name ties these pairs to a classic model of strong electron interaction. Control here is fast, on ultrafast time scales.

The team frames a broad goal: control of the many-body wave function of a quantum material. Such control could give scientists a precise knob for new states of matter. It could also serve quantum sensing, which uses quantum effects to measure with great care. The paper works at the joint of light, matter, and quantum control. It shows how short light pulses can shape what excitons do.
arxiv-2601-20895:
Luca Pinchetti and three co-authors speed up a brain-inspired way to train neural networks. Their 2026 paper concerns predictive coding networks. Research on neuroscience-inspired learning algorithms is accelerating. Energy-based methods like predictive coding draw much of this interest. They are versatile and rest on firm math. Their weakness is cost: the iterative way they learn is slow.

The authors attack that cost through better initialization. A smarter start can cut the rounds the network must run. That trims the compute each training step demands. Faster predictive coding would make the method practical at larger scales. It could then compete with standard training on real tasks. The work speaks to researchers who want learning rules closer to the brain's own.
arxiv-2601-21095:
A. A. Jafari, C. Ozcinar, and G. Anbarjafari survey responsible AI with a deliberately even hand. Their 2026 paper reviews the rapid spread of artificial intelligence across organizations. That spread brings profound strategic opportunities. It also introduces significant ethical and operational risks. Scholarly attention to responsible AI has grown with the spread. The literature, though, remains fragmented. Much of it leans optimistic, stressing value creation. Other work leans excessively cautious, fixated on harms.

The title's three-part frame organizes the review: the good, the bad, and the AI itself. The authors aim for a balanced account between hype and fear. Fragmented advice leaves managers without a coherent playbook. A unified view can guide real adoption choices. The paper was submitted to the Journal of Strategic Information Systems. It speaks to leaders weighing AI's promise against its perils.
arxiv-2601-21195:
Arvind Ayyer, Sarah Brauner, Jan de Gier, and Anne Schilling study a classic shuffling process and its deformed versions. In the Tsetlin library, books sit on a shelf and each book is pulled to the front with its own fixed chance. The process is a clean model of random reordering.

The authors extend the process with a two-parameter deformation drawn from modern algebra. Such deformations often reveal hidden structure in the original model. They track how the long-run behavior changes under the new rules. The work links a simple shelf model to deep questions about symmetry and random motion.
arxiv-2601-21495:
Edoardo Otranto groups countries by how their temperatures change over time. The study uses yearly temperature data for a large set of countries across more than a century. Three grouping methods are tried, each built on a different view of the warming pattern.

One method groups by warming rate, one by year-to-year swings, and one by how long swings keep the same sign. Two distance measures feed the groupings. Space-time models then describe each group's shared pattern. Grouping similar climates together helps researchers model warming with fewer, cleaner patterns instead of one noisy model per country.
arxiv-2601-21695:
Shihao Weng, Yang Feng, Jincheng Li, Yining Yin, Xiaofei Xie, and Jia Liu fix transformer models by patching their attention. Models hit by backdoor attacks or bias often show odd attention patterns. They stare too hard at trigger tokens or at protected traits.

Older neuron-editing fixes are rigid and can warp the model's features. The authors hot-fix the over-attention directly, in the spirit of a software patch. A targeted patch should remove the bad behavior while leaving honest skills intact. The approach suits deployed models, where retraining from scratch is too slow when a flaw is found.
arxiv-2601-21895:
Hongyi Zhou and co-authors build tools to detect text written by large language models. Systems such as GPT, Claude, and Gemini now produce prose that reads as human. That fluency raises real concerns about misinformation and academic integrity, and it creates urgent demand for reliable detection.

Their 2026 preprint proposes learning distances between texts, so that machine-written and human writing sit measurably apart. A distance-based detector can flag suspect passages without needing the generating model itself. Detection will never be perfect, but dependable methods help schools, publishers, and platforms enforce their rules. The work joins a fast-moving contest between generation and detection that shows no sign of slowing.
arxiv-2601-22095:
Chuanyang Zheng and co-authors rethink where normalization layers belong in a Transformer. Designers must choose between normalizing before each block or after it, the Pre-Norm and Post-Norm layouts. Each has known quirks, and the choice has stayed an open question in architecture design.

The authors view the question through manifold optimization. The outputs of the attention and feed-forward layers are treated as update directions in an optimization problem living on a curved space. Their 2026 preprint, GeoNorm, uses geodesic optimization to unify the two layouts in one scheme. A principled settlement of this small design question could stabilize training across the huge models built on the Transformer pattern.
arxiv-2601-22495:
Gudrun Thorkelsdottir and Arindam Banerjee tune flow matching models in slow, gentle steps. Flow matching models learn to turn noise into data along a smooth path. Their 2026 preprint notes that free, hard tuning on small or shifting data can erase what pretraining won.

Gradual tuning moves the model in small, staged shifts instead. The aim is to keep past gains while still fitting the new task. That balance matters where data are scarce or drift over time. It also saves compute. The work offers a careful path for a fast-growing model class.
arxiv-2601-22795:
Corentin Kervadec, Iuliia Lysova, Marco Baroni, and Gemma Boleda ask whether big language models use all of their parts evenly. These models hold billions of settings spread across deep, wide networks. Past work found that many settings can be cut with little loss, which hints that work is spread unevenly.

The authors measure how dense the computation is across the model, part by part. Knowing which parts do the real work can guide pruning, the careful removal of unused settings. That in turn can make large models cheaper and faster to run.
arxiv-2601-22895:
Aya Laajil and three co-authors work on forecasts that predict several outcomes at once, with honest doubt. A good forecast distribution should be sharp yet calibrated, matching how often events really occur. That balance is well studied for single outcomes, but much harder for many at once.

Their method builds on pre-rank functions, which squash a multi-outcome forecast into a single score for checking. They use those scores during training, not just as an after-the-fact check. Better calibrated joint forecasts matter for weather, energy, and risk planning.
arxiv-2604-01195:
Nandan Thakur and co-authors present ORBIT in 2026, a system for training search agents. Search agents join language models with web search for hard questions. Building training data for deep research tasks remains costly and hard.

Such tasks involve multi-step retrieval and reasoning over many sources. Human annotation is expensive, and other routes carry cumbersome prerequisites, they note. ORBIT aims at scalable and verifiable data generation on a tight budget. Its title promises exactly that economy with checks on quality. Cheaper, verified training data could widen who can build research agents. The paper speaks to teams training agents without large annotation budgets. It treats data generation itself as the bottleneck to solve.

balzac-colonel-chabert-marriage-1895:
Colonel Chabert was left for dead on the field of Eylau, buried under corpses, yet he lived. Balzac's short novel, in Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell's 1895 version, follows his return to Paris. His wife has married again and holds his fortune, and the law sees no easy way to raise a dead man.

A young lawyer takes the case, and pity fights paperwork through the tale. Chabert's end ranks among the saddest in the Human Comedy, a whole epic of war and loss in miniature. Many readers call it Balzac's most perfect short work, proof of how much he could hold in few pages.
balzac-country-doctor-marriage-1895:
Doctor Benassis arrives in a poor Savoy village and quietly rebuilds it, road by road and field by field. The Country Doctor, translated by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell in 1895, is Balzac's most hopeful provincial novel. It answers his Paris books, where greed rules, with a tale of patient public good.

Through talks with soldiers, peasants, and a dying water-carrier's son, Benassis shares his creed of work and order. His own buried sorrow explains the zeal that drives him. The novel, Le Médecin de campagne in French, remains the Human Comedy's great statement of what one devoted life can mend.
balzac-cousin-pons-marriage-1895:
Sylvain Pons loves music and old art, and asks little from life but meals at his cousins' table. Cousin Pons, in Ellen Marriage's 1895 translation, shows what happens when his quiet collection of pictures and curios gains real value. Relatives who once mocked him turn hunters, and the kind man has no defense ready.

Paired with Cousin Bette as Les Parents pauvres, the poor relations, this is among Balzac's darkest late novels. Greed works here through lawyers, dealers, and family duty, all smiling as they close in. Pons and his friend Schmucke stand as two innocents in a Paris that prices everything, even loyalty.
balzac-lost-illusions-marriage-1895:
Lucien de Rubempré leaves his small town for Paris with a poet's hopes, and Balzac's Lost Illusions tracks what the city does to him. Ellen Marriage's 1895 English version holds all three parts of the novel. At its heart stands the world of newspapers, where praise and ruin are both for sale.

Balzac shows printing shops, paper mills, and newsrooms as one great machine for grinding reputations. Lucien learns its rules too late, at a cost to everyone near him. Readers rank the book at the center of the Human Comedy, Balzac's vast portrait of French life after Napoleon.
balzac-magic-skin-marriage-1895:
A young man finds a strange piece of skin in a Paris antique shop, and The Magic Skin grants him every wish. Each wish, though, shrinks the skin, and with it his remaining life. Balzac's tale, La Peau de chagrin, made his name and anchors the thoughtful side of the Human Comedy.

Ellen Marriage translated the novel in 1895, and her version keeps its mix of wild fancy and sharp Paris detail. The hero must choose between wanting and living, a bargain no wealth can soften. Few novels state Balzac's great theme so cleanly: desire itself spends the life it feeds on.
balzac-pere-goriot-marriage-1895:
Honoré de Balzac wrote Father Goriot in French, and Ellen Marriage made it English in 1895. Marriage's version served J. M. Dent's landmark full Comédie Humaine in English dress. The novel of Parisian ambition sits near the heart of Balzac's vast human comedy.

Old Goriot, a rich pasta maker ruined by his daughters' greed, fades in a boarding house. Young Rastignac, a law student, learns Paris ways from the smooth rogue Vautrin there. Goriot dies calling for daughters who send empty carriages to his pauper's grave in Paris. Rastignac buries him and turns to face the city he vows to conquer next. Balzac maps money, rank, and family love with a surgeon's cold, clear eye.
balzac-the-thirteen-wormeley-marriage-18:
Thirteen men, bound by a secret pact, move through Balzac's Paris like a hidden government. The Thirteen gathers three tales, Ferragus, The Duchess of Langeais, and The Girl with the Golden Eyes, in the 1895 Wormeley and Marriage translations. Each story tests what the brotherhood will do for one of its own.

Love, kidnapping, and revenge drive the plots, while the thirteen hover at the edges, rich and unseen. Balzac gives his Human Comedy a conspiratorial heart here, a Paris beneath Paris. The trilogy mixes melodrama with his usual sharp eye for money, rank, and desire.
bekker-world-bewitched-1695:
Balthasar Bekker strikes at the Devil's power in The World Bewitch'd, in English from 1695. Bekker was a church man in Holland who used the new thought of Descartes. Spirits, he holds, can't push flesh: a soul with no bulk can't move a chair, sign a pact, or ride a broom through the night sky of his cold north land.

His four books take on witch trials, ghosts, and the Good Book's own tales. The church cast him out for it, yet his case spread. The book is a chief blow that broke the hunts. Its nerve still awes.
beowulf-morris-wyatt-1895:
William Morris and A. J. Wyatt gave English readers a new Beowulf in 1895, in the fine Kelmscott Press edition. Their text turns the Old English epic into rich, old-style verse. Beowulf, a hero from Geatland, sails to Denmark to help King Hrothgar.

Grendel, his mother, and a dragon that guards a hoard give the hero three great fights. The last fight costs Beowulf his life, and his people mourn a brave king. Morris loved old tales and fine books, and his version feels like both. It links the medieval poem to modern readers. Scholars still use it to feel the poem's rough music.

Scraps and short tracts by H. P. Blavatsky fill A Modern Panarion, a set put out in 1895, past her death. She wrote for small tracts and weeklies through her career. Much of that work was hard to find. This set saves the best of it in one place.

Her voice here is sharp and game for a fight. She defends her creed, mocks its foes, and glosses hard points in brief. The set rounds out the shelf of her main books. It shows the fierce hand that built a world wide creed. The name Panarion comes from a saint's chest of cures for false creeds. Blavatsky's heirs chose it to claim her scraps held like worth.

William Wynn Westcott edited the Chaldaean Oracles of Zoroaster for English readers in 1895. The Oracles are fragments of Greek verse preserved by Neoplatonic philosophers. Tradition ascribed them to Zoroaster, though they date from the Roman era.

The fragments teach theurgy, the ritual work of rising toward the divine. Fire, the father, and the soul's ascent dominate the surviving lines. Neoplatonists prized these sayings above almost all other texts. Westcott gathered them with commentary for the occult revival's students. His edition overlaps his Collectanea Hermetica volume on the same text. The double publication shows how central the Oracles were to Golden Dawn teaching.

Hastur, Carcosa, and the Lake of Hali haunt the tales as names half grasped. Those hints let each fan build the myth in their own mind.
