The authors offer a model-based Bayesian approach instead, with a step that selects which factors matter. Bayesian methods weigh evidence in a structured way and can handle the mess of large compendium data sets. A better search tool helps biologists pull real gene partnerships out of thousands of experiments. That can reveal control networks that single experiments, taken alone, would never show.
plos-pone-0004595:
When cells sound the heat shock alarm, two helper proteins join forces, show Sarah Gibbs, Brandy Barren, Katy Beck, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. After a conditioning stress, cells raise their levels of molecular chaperones called heat shock proteins. These helpers protect other proteins from damage. In neurons, chaperones guard against ischemia, the loss of blood flow, and against neurodegenerative diseases.

The partners here are Hsp40 and the CSPalpha chaperone complex, which works at nerve endings. The team shows Hsp40 couples with that complex upon induction of the heat shock response. A stress-triggered partnership helps explain how nerve terminals survive insults. It may also offer a handle for protecting neurons in stroke and degeneration.
plos-pone-0004695:
Gordon Ng and colleagues found a new enzyme that recycles hydrogen made when bacteria fix nitrogen, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fixing nitrogen from air also makes hydrogen gas in equal amounts. Some bacteria that live on air nitrogen use a known enzyme to reclaim that hydrogen at the cell surface.

The team reports a second, inner route that does the same job. Finding a new path changes how the energy books of these bacteria are read. It may also help efforts to grow crops or make fuel with less waste. Small gains in reuse can add up at farm scale.
plos-pone-0004795:
Hiroyuki Hamada and colleagues built a framework linking cell cycle arrest and cell death based on p53 dynamics, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tumor suppressor p53 regulates genes for DNA repair, cycle arrest, and programmed death. It can trigger both arrest and death, yet how it specifies which outcome a given damaged cell will take was not clear before this modeling.

The team modeled p53 pulses over time and their downstream effects. Dynamics, not just level, appear to frame the choice. A clearer framework helps predict cancer cell responses. It may guide drugs that push cells toward death.
plos-pone-0004895:
Linda Dong and colleagues analyzed growth, differentiation, and apoptosis genes with risk of renal cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The case control study enrolled nearly a thousand renal cancer cases and more controls in Central and Eastern Europe. Genomic DNA was analyzed for hundreds of tagging variants in twenty one genes involved in cellular growth. Testing used high throughput genotyping platforms and standard statistical methods.

Specific variants modestly alter renal cancer susceptibility. Kidney cancer has strong environmental components too. Combined genetic profiles improve risk models slightly. European data fill population gaps. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004995:
PCA3 is a gene switched on almost only in prostate cancer. That makes it a prized biomarker. Raymond Clarke and colleagues investigated its genomic organization in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used cDNA synthesis and related methods. The goal was to understand PCA3's importance for detection and progression.

They found a new genomic structure for the gene. PCA3 sits nested within a larger gene, BMCC1. The corrected map changes how the marker should be read. Tests that measure PCA3 depend on knowing its true layout. The finding refines a tool doctors use against prostate cancer. It also raises new questions about how the two nested genes interact.
plos-pone-0005095:
Flu vaccine recipes are set each year for each hemisphere. Brazil straddles the tropics, where flu timing is messy. Wyller Alencar de Mello and colleagues examined the dilemma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Since 1999, the World Health Organization issues an extra recommendation for the Southern Hemisphere. Brazil's fit with that system was the question.

The study tested alternative scenarios for Brazil. Different recipes and timings gave different results. One-size-fits-all policy fails at the equator. A tropical country may need its own schedule. The analysis helps Brazil choose with evidence. It also warns other tropical nations. Borrowing temperate-zone vaccine policy can waste shots and leave people unprotected.
plos-pone-0005195:
Strong lifestyle programs can cut heart disease risk in tight research trials. The open question is whether those gains survive in everyday primary care clinics. Eriksson and colleagues ran a three-year randomized trial in Sweden, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009, called the Björknäs study.

Patients in ordinary clinics took part in an intensive lifestyle program aimed at heart risk. The trial tested whether the benefits of costly, controlled programs can transfer to routine care. Its results matter for health systems that must decide if such programs are worth funding at scale.
plos-pone-0005295:
Red algae and most cyanobacteria harvest light with antenna complexes called phycobilisomes. In cyanobacteria, those antennas were thought to drift across the membrane surface. Liu and colleagues tested that mobility in a red alga in PLOS ONE in 2009 using a fluorescence method called FRAP.

FRAP tracks how fluorescence returns to a bleached spot. The recovery came from intrinsic light processes inside the phycobilisomes, not from large-scale diffusion of the antennas. So in red algae the antennas largely stay put, correcting the picture of how these organisms gather light. How sea plants catch light sets how much food the whole sea food web can make, so a fix to this small point shifts a much larger picture.
plos-pone-0005395:
Anaplastic thyroid cancer is one of the most lethal human cancers, with mean survival of about six months. Finding the cells that start these tumors is a priority. Friedman and colleagues identified such cells by a surface marker, CD133, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

CD133-positive cells from this cancer initiated tumors in immunodeficient mice. The hormone thyrotropin also regulated those cells. A defined cancer-initiating population gives researchers a target for drugs against a cancer that resists nearly everything tried so far. Most thyroid cancers are mild, but this kind is not, and its speed leaves little time to test drugs. So a known target cell found in weeks is a strong gain for labs in this field.
plos-pone-0005495:
Ryu Takizawa and colleagues linked a gene to brain activity in schizophrenia in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Brain scans can show gene effects more directly than symptoms can. A gene called COMT affects how fast the brain clears dopamine, a key signal for thought.

The team scanned the front of the brain while people with schizophrenia did thinking tasks. They compared blood flow patterns across forms of the COMT gene. The link they found helps show how a small gene change can shape brain function in mental illness, even before symptoms are considered.
plos-pone-0005595:
Clara Francí and co-authors proposed a new marker for colon tumours in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A gene called Snail1 helps normal cells change form during development. In cancer, that same change can help tumour cells spread.

The team looked for the Snail1 protein not in the tumour cells but in the tissue around them, using a new antibody tool. Protein in that surrounding tissue marked patients with a worse outlook. A marker in the tumour's neighbourhood could help doctors choose how hard to treat. Markers drawn from routine tumour samples are the easiest kind for hospitals to adopt.
plos-pone-0005695:
Marc Cadotte and colleagues tested in 2009 what makes plant groups grow more total mass. Twenty years of trials show that more plant species in a plot often means more growth. The standard claim is that varied traits let plants share light, water, and soil more fully.

The team compared three kinds of diversity: family-tree distance, working traits, and trait spread. They asked which one best predicts how much a plant community yields. The answer helps farmers and land managers pick seed mixes that truly boost growth. It also sharpens the science of why diversity matters at all.
plos-pone-0005795:
Yi Ren and co-authors built a combined gene and chromosome map of the cucumber genome in 2009. Cucumbers belong to a crop family with melons, squash, and pumpkins, yet shared genomic tools were scarce. Cucumber's narrow genetic base also made dense maps hard to build.

The integrated map lines up DNA markers with visible chromosome features. Breeders can now locate traits, like disease resistance, on a stable frame. The resource serves the whole cucurbit family, not just cucumber growers. Better maps shorten the path from a wild trait to a farm-ready variety.
plos-pone-0005895:
Mathieu Dubrulle and co-authors timed in 2009 how fast chikungunya virus becomes infectious in mosquito saliva. Two Aedes species spread this virus, which causes fever and joint pain outbreaks. A recent variant with a surface change spreads better through one of the species.

Mosquito saliva turned infectious as soon as two days after the mosquito's blood meal, they found. Such a short wait means outbreaks can ignite quickly once mosquitoes bite an infected person. The timing refines risk models used when cases appear. It also shows why rapid mosquito control matters in the first days of an outbreak.
plos-pone-0005995:
Pairing a brain chemical with sight can leave a lasting mark on the visual brain. Jun Il Kang and Elvire Vaucher tested that pairing in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper joins acetylcholine, a chemical tied to learning, with visual activation, and then measures the brain's electrical answer to sight in the primary visual cortex.

The paired input raised those answers for a long term, the title reports. A boost that lasts suggests the pairing rewires how strongly the cortex answers what the eye sees. The work adds to the case that acetylcholine gates lasting change in the adult brain, a finding with weight for learning and for recovery after brain injury.
plos-pone-0006095:
Sperm must sense their surroundings precisely to reach and enter an egg. Gerardo De Blas, Alberto Darszon, Ana Ocampo and colleagues characterized one of their sensors in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies TRPM8 in human sperm, a member of the TRP channel family, more than thirty proteins that translate heat, chemicals and force into calcium signals.

TRPM8 proves versatile in sperm, the title reports, answering more than one kind of cue. A channel with several jobs in one small cell is a strong lead for fertility science. Understanding it could help explain some male infertility and might one day offer a target for a male contraceptive that blocks a single channel.
plos-pone-0006195:
Sequencing has handed scientists the full protein lists of many disease germs, yet new drugs remain scarce. David Toomey, Heinrich Hoppe, and Marian Brennan present Genomes2Drugs in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The challenge is picking, from thousands of proteins, the few that make good drug targets.

The tool combines protein data with gene activity data to rank likely targets and lead drugs. It narrows a flood of lab output into a short list worth testing. Faster shortlists matter most for neglected diseases with small research budgets. The paper shows how computing can steer scarce lab time toward the best bets.
plos-pone-0006295:
Hearing is not symmetric: one brain side often leads, and sound meaning can tip the balance. Muriel Basile, Alban Lemasson, and Catherine Blois-Heulin compared humans with Campbell's monkeys in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Social and emotional value of sounds had already been shown to influence which hemisphere dominates listening.

Both species showed auditory laterality shaped by familiarity and feeling in the sounds. Shared patterns between humans and monkeys hint at deep roots for language's brain layout. Language is usually left-led in humans, and its origins remain debated. Primate comparisons like this supply evidence that animal studies can offer.
plos-pone-0006395:
Taste research leaned on rodents for decades, leaving primate taste almost unmapped. Peter Hevezi and colleagues performed a genome-wide analysis of gene expression in primate taste buds in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their work is the first comprehensive characterisation of its kind for primates.

The expression profile reveals links from taste buds to diverse other processes. Taste tissue expresses genes with jobs far beyond flavour. Those links suggest taste buds double as sensors for body state. Primate data also correct assumptions borrowed from mice. The work opens fresh lines of study on what taste buds do for the whole body.
plos-pone-0006495:
Andreas Doncic, Eshel Ben-Jacob, Shmuel Einav, and colleagues reverse-engineered a cell safety system in PLOS ONE in 2009. The spindle assembly checkpoint ensures proper chromosome segregation during cell division. It works by inhibiting Cdc20, a co-factor that would otherwise trigger the separation step. If the checkpoint fails, cells can gain or lose chromosomes.

Reverse engineering means inferring the system's design from its behavior. The authors model how the checkpoint senses unattached chromosomes and holds the division machinery back. A clear model explains how such a vital guard stays both sensitive and reliable. Errors in this system are tied to cancer and birth defects.
plos-pone-0006595:
Laurence Flori and co-authors read the genome's response to breeding in dairy cattle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dairy cattle breeds have been subjected over fifty years to intense artificial selection for milk production traits. The team performed a genome-wide study of that selection. Selected regions carry signatures in DNA variation.

Their case study shows which parts of the genome responded to artificial selection. Milk traits improved dramatically, and the genome records how. Knowing selected regions helps breeders manage diversity while improving yield. It also offers a model for studying selection in other domesticated species.
plos-pone-0006695:
Merav Darash-Yahana and colleagues examined a signaling pair linked to cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pair is the chemokine CXCL16 and its receptor CXCR6. Chemokines guide white blood cells through the body. Clinical observations and mouse work had suggested that inflammation can help tumors grow. The authors suspected chemokines play central roles in cancers tied to inflammation.

The team screened prostate tissue for dozens of chemokines. They then followed up on CXCL16 and CXCR6 as markers of disease. Their results also cast the pair as promoters, not just bystanders. A marker that also drives growth is doubly useful to researchers. It could guide both cancer detection and future treatment design.
plos-pone-0006795:
Delphine Destoumieux-Garzón and colleagues studied an immune protein family in a moth in PLOS ONE in 2009. The insect is Spodoptera frugiperda, the fall armyworm. Its X-tox proteins appear only in butterflies and moths. They consist of repeated defensin-like motifs strung together. Earlier family-tree work suggested X-tox evolved from ancestral defensins.

Defensins normally kill microbes as part of immunity. The X-tox protein has lost that ancestral function, as the title reports. Its repeat structure earned it the nickname defensin rosary. Losing a killing function while keeping the shape is an evolutionary puzzle. The case shows immune proteins can be repurposed over time.
plos-pone-0006895:
Marc Lipsitch and colleagues estimated the true scale of the 2009 flu outbreak in Mexico in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus was novel influenza A/H1N1. Accurate case totals and severity are needed early in an epidemic. Early counts capture mostly severe cases seen at hospitals. Mild cases at home go uncounted, skewing severity upward.

Foreign travelers offered an indirect measuring stick. Their infections in Mexico could be counted more completely after return. From traveler incidence, the authors estimated lower bounds for Mexico's cumulative incidence. A defensible floor helps officials size the epidemic honestly. The method can serve future outbreaks where local counting lags behind spread.
plos-pone-0006995:
Paritha Arumugam, Fabrizia Urbinati, Chinavenmeni Velu, and colleagues dissected a genetic insulator in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulators are DNA elements that fence off active gene regions. They stop silencing chromatin from spreading into working genes. The chicken HS4 element is the classic test case for insulator research.

Earlier work mapped two key motifs in the element's core region. This team studied its tail end, the three prime region. That tail shared properties with the core and proved needed for full strength. Knowing all working parts matters for gene therapy, where insulators protect inserted genes.
plos-pone-0007095:
David Cantu, Jerome Schaack, and Manisha Patel studied neuron damage in cell cultures in PLOS ONE in 2009. Oxidative stress inside mitochondria contributes to many neuronal disorders. Exactly how reactive oxygen species kill neurons was still unknown. The team focused on aconitase, a mitochondrial enzyme easily damaged by oxidation.

They used rat primary mesencephalic cultures, which include dopamine neurons. When aconitase was oxidatively shut down, iron and hydrogen peroxide drove toxicity. That chain offers a concrete route from rust-like chemistry to cell death. It is relevant to Parkinson's disease, where these neurons die.
plos-pone-0007195:
Darryl R. Davis, Yiqiang Zhang, Rachel R. Smith, and colleagues validated a method for growing heart progenitor cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. At least four labs had grown such cells directly from adult heart tissue. The cells form spheres called cardiospheres, which yield cardiosphere-derived cells for study.

Those derived cells were already being tested in a clinical trial when the paper appeared. The authors check whether the cardiosphere method reliably cultures cardiac progenitor cells from heart muscle tissue. Their validation matters for heart repair research that depends on consistent cell batches.
plos-pone-0007295:
Maxim A. Khasnatinov, Katarina Ustanikova, Tatiana V. Frolova, and colleagues studied tick-borne encephalitis virus strains in 2009. The virus causes epidemics across Eurasia. Illness ranges from silent infection and fever to fatal brain inflammation, but factors deciding severity were undefined when the study appeared.

The virus normally agglutinates red blood cells in standard tests. The authors study non-hemagglutinating flaviviruses that lost that trait. They examine molecular mechanisms behind new strains adapting to European ticks. Their work links small viral changes to altered behavior in laboratory tests and possibly in human disease.
plos-pone-0007395:
Theresa Casey, Osman Patel, Karl Dykema, and colleagues found clock gene signatures in lactation biology in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Genes linked to lactation evolved more slowly than other mammalian genes. Milk and mammary genes are highly conserved, suggesting species differences in milk come partly from environment and deeper regulation in the genome.

The authors search molecular signatures of that regulation. They report circadian clocks may orchestrate the homeorhetic response to lactation. Homeorhesis is the coordinated shift of body resources toward milk production. Daily clocks timing that shift could affect milk yield in dairy animals.
plos-pone-0007495:
Aude Legoffic and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 hunting for genes that change early in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is deadly largely because it is found late. The team scanned tumor DNA with an ultra-high-resolution microarray. Their goal was to spot genes whose copy number changes in the earliest stages. Early changes are the best candidates for detection markers and drug targets.

One gene stood out: reg4. It is amplified, copied extra times, in the early stages of the cancer's development. A gene switched on that early could flag disease before symptoms appear. It could also serve as a target for new therapies. The authors present reg4 as a promising candidate on both counts. For a cancer with few options, an early lever like this is valuable.
plos-pone-0007595:
Min Tan and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on mating behavior in the short-nosed fruit bat. Oral sex is widely used in human foreplay but rarely documented in other animals. It had been recorded in bonobos, mostly as play among young males. The fruit bat Cynopterus sphinx shows a different pattern, with females performing fellatio during copulation itself. The team measured what that behavior accomplishes.

Females that performed fellatio extended the length of copulation. Longer mating likely improves the chance of fertilization. So the behavior carries a clear reproductive payoff, not just social play. Documenting a purpose separates this case from anecdotes. The study adds a rare, measured example of oral sex in a wild mammal. It also shows how mating behaviors can be tested for function, not merely noted.
plos-pone-0007695:
Hanna Fredholm and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns breast cancer in young women. The disease is uncommon before middle age, yet it is the most frequent cancer in women under forty. Young patients also tend to fare worse than older ones.

The team measured survival in young women and asked how much of the gap strong treatment could close. Their answer, summed in the title, is sobering. Even with intensive treatment, young women died at higher rates. The study makes the case for research aimed at the distinct biology of early breast cancer.
plos-pone-0007795:
Maris Kuningas and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests an evolutionary idea about inflammation in a Ghanaian population. Chronic inflammation feeds many diseases of aging. Yet strong inflammatory responses help young people survive infections.

Under harsh conditions, natural selection may favor genes that inflame readily. Those same genes can harm their carriers later in life. The authors looked for signs of such selection in Ghana. Their data link adverse environments to selection for pro-inflammatory variation. The study connects infection pressure in youth to disease risk in old age.
plos-pone-0007895:
Meng-Hua Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It checks real parentage in the three-toed woodpecker. Molecular tools have shown bird mating systems are more complex than they look. Social pairs do not always match genetic parents.

Using microsatellite markers, the team determined the chicks' true parents. They measured how common extrapair paternity was in this species. They also looked for maternity surprises, such as quasi-parasitism. The results add a northern woodland species to the parentage map. Such data test theories about why birds seek mates outside the pair.
plos-pone-0007995:
Ruth Reef, Paulina Kaniewska, and Ove Hoegh-Guldberg tested coral skeletons as sun shields in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reef corals live in bright, shallow tropic seas and host light-loving partners in their tissue. Too much ultraviolet light can harm both host and partner.

The skeleton under the living tissue blocks and scatters a large share of that harsh light. The coral thus lives behind a built-in shield of its own making. As seas warm and stress mounts, knowing this defense exists helps judge which corals may cope and which may bleach first.
plos-pone-0008095:
Valerie Walshe and colleagues taught a computer to predict immune display pieces for one molecule in PLOS ONE in 2009. The molecule, HLA-Cw*0102, grabs protein bits inside cells and shows them to immune scouts. Predicting which bits it grabs is a core step in computer-aided vaccine design.

The team paired model building with dish tests until the forecasts held up. This form of the molecule had been poorly charted, leaving a blind spot in vaccine planning. A trusty predictor fills the gap and may reveal fresh vaccine targets on germs and tumors alike.
plos-pone-0008195:
Ana M. Tortajada, María José Carmona, and Manuel Serra asked an evolution question in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inbreeding often lowers fitness, a cost called inbreeding depression. When a few founders colonize a new habitat, that cost can shape what happens next. Later arrivals may gain an edge because their hybrid offspring are fitter. Rotifers, tiny water animals, offer a test case.

Many rotifers reproduce under a system called haplodiploidy. The authors asked whether that system purges the harmful effects of inbreeding. Their answer bears on how populations survive founding events. It also informs wider theory about mating systems and genetic load.
plos-pone-0008295:
Bernd Binder, Andrean Goede, and Nikolaus Berndt built a math model of cell organelles in PLOS ONE in 2009. Organelles form, degrade, and renew in a constant dynamic process. Vesicles bud, fuse, and travel between organelles without pause. Regulatory proteins such as SNAREs, Rabs, and coats run this traffic. Given such complex machinery, how organelles keep distinct identities is controversial.

Their conceptual model explores the dynamic self-organisation of distinct organelles. Math can test whether simple rules explain stable compartments. If so, cell structure emerges from traffic itself. The work bridges cell biology and systems theory.
plos-pone-0008395:
Takahiro Soshi and colleagues studied time perception and sleep in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. Human perception of short time intervals varies across the day. It generally fluctuates in step with the circadian clock. Sleep deprivation seems to modulate that diurnal variation. The team used near-infrared spectroscopy to image the prefrontal cortex during timing tasks.

Sleep deprivation changed both time perception and prefrontal activity. The prefrontal area supports attention and working memory needed for timing. Their link shows how tired brains misjudge time. The findings matter for shift workers and safety-critical jobs.
plos-pone-0008495:
Bin Su and co-authors study two flu virus proteins in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Influenza A has a surface protein called hemagglutinin, or HA. HA binds host cells and drives the fusion that lets virus enter. Another protein, neuraminidase or NA, cuts those binding sugars. Its known job was to free new viruses from infected cells. The team test if NA also helps entry.

They find NA enhances HA-mediated cell fusion and virus entry. That gives NA a second role at the start of infection. Entry and release are thus linked by the same protein pair. The finding may matter for antiviral drugs that target NA.
plos-pone-0008595:
Trygve Leergaard and co-authors validate diffusion MRI in rat brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Diffusion MRI measures microstructural features of brain white matter. Common measures have limited capacity to resolve complex fiber orientations. Several promising new approaches aim to map fiber orientation distributions better. Validation against real anatomy is essential before trusting them. The team use quantitative histology, microscopic tissue analysis, as ground truth. They compare MRI fiber estimates with histological fiber maps in rat brain.

Their validation shows where diffusion MRI orientations match real fibers. It also shows where the method still errs in complex crossings. That benchmark helps improve brain mapping for research and medicine.
plos-pone-0008695:
Ke Hao, Eugene Chudin, Danielle Greenawalt, and colleagues measured a hidden bias in gene hunting. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looks at genome-wide association studies, called GWAS. These studies scan many people for DNA links to disease. Hidden ancestry differences between groups can fake a link. The team wanted the real size of that problem.

They compared liver samples from groups of different ancestries. The samples came from hundreds of donors in the United States. Their measures show how strongly ancestry can skew results. They also show what that skew does to study findings. Gene hunters can use the numbers to correct their work.
plos-pone-0008795:
Shannon Manning, A. Cody Springman, Amber Million, and colleagues tested whether cows pass a risky germ to people. Their prospective study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Group B Streptococcus can colonize healthy adults silently. It can also cause severe illness in newborns. Suspicion long held that cattle were the original source. DNA comparisons, though, suggested human and cow strains mostly stay apart.

The team compared colonization in people with and without bovine contact. Exposure patterns were checked against who carried the germ. Direct evidence helps settle a long-running source debate. The answer guides farm and maternity infection control.
plos-pone-0008895:
Brice Semmens, Peter Auster, and Michelle Paddack tested whether networks of ocean reserves can truly protect sea life. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Marine protected areas are a leading plan for saving ocean diversity. Networks of reserves should shelter species better than single parks. Diversity patterns, though, can complicate where reserves help most. Null models provide a fair baseline: what chance alone would protect.

Comparing real networks against those baselines showed their true added value. Some network designs beat chance clearly, while others barely did. Honest auditing prevents reserves that look good only on maps. Conservation funds can then chase designs that beat the baseline.
plos-pone-0008995:
David Metzgar and co-authors built one test that names many flu viruses at once, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most human flu A infections come from just two subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2. Birds, though, carry a wide store of flu A types and new variants. Spotting a bird variant early in people is key to stopping a pandemic.

The single assay detects flu types and subtypes in one run. It can tell human strains from avian ones and flag emerging variants. Older testing needed separate runs for each of those questions. A faster, broader test strengthens the surveillance net for new flu threats.
plos-pone-0009095:
Heleen Rienstra and co-authors tracked gel-like matrix proteins as transplanted rat kidneys healed and scarred, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most late kidney graft losses come from chronic transplant dysfunction. The graft slowly remodels, with scarred vessels and fibrous tissue. Proteoglycans are matrix proteins that manage cell contacts and tissue structure.

The team measured proteoglycan patterns after experimental kidney transplantation. Different family members rose or fell as remodelling proceeded. New lymph vessels growing into the graft followed the same story. Matrix shifts like these may flag grafts heading for chronic failure.
plos-pone-0009195:
Ann Walsh, David Langley, Richard Colonno, and co-authors published this virology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines entecavir, a drug used against hepatitis B virus. Entecavir blocks the viral polymerase, the enzyme the virus uses to copy its DNA. In clinics, the virus rarely learns to resist the drug.

The team combined lab experiments with computer modeling of the polymerase. They worked out, step by step, how entecavir stops DNA copying with delayed chain termination. They also examined what changes the virus would need to escape the drug. Multiple required changes help explain why resistance stays rare, which supports entecavir as a durable treatment.
plos-pone-0009295:
Elizabeth Smith and co-authors published this cell signaling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The MAPK pathway carries growth signals from the cell surface to the nucleus. Textbooks held that once switched on, MAPK slips into the nucleus freely to adjust genes. The authors found that picture does not hold everywhere.

In primary ovarian and mammary epithelial cells, activated MAPK was kept out of the nucleus. The restriction appeared in normal cells taken straight from tissue, not in lab-adapted lines. That difference warns that cell lines can mislead about how signals work in the body. It also adds a control point to a pathway often hijacked in cancer.
plos-pone-0009395:
Yehuda Ben-Shahar and co-authors published this fly gene study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A family of channels called Deg/ENaC lets cells sense touch, salt, and pain signals. These channels pass sodium and ignore voltage, staying ready at all times. Their work is fine-tuned by helper proteins.

The team studied a fruit fly gene called CheB42a. They found it modifies how Deg/ENaC channels function. A modifier gene matters because it can dial a channel's output up or down. Such tuning helps explain how the same channel family serves so many different senses.
plos-pone-0009495:
Yiwen Li, Weng Tao, and Lingyu Luo tested a growth factor in rat eyes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cone cells give us color sight and sharp central vision. In diseases like retinitis pigmentosa, cones decay late in the disease and central sight is lost. The team gave a protein called CNTF to rats with retinal decay. They watched the light catching tips of the cones.

CNTF led damaged cones to regrow their outer segments, the parts that catch light. Regrowth of that kind had not been shown so clearly before. The work offers a lead toward saving sight by repair, not just by slowing loss. It will need much more testing before use in people.
plos-pone-0009595:
Christian Quaia, Howard Ying, and Lance Optican measured eye muscle mechanics in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2010. The muscles that move the eye must stretch and recoil with great precision. A stretched muscle pushes back with a force that depends on its history of movement. The team applied natural patterns of stretch to passive eye muscles. They recorded the forces that resulted.

The force depended mostly on the most recent stretch, not the whole past sequence. That finding supports a simpler model of how these muscles behave. Precise models matter for eye surgery and for tools that track gaze. This study is the third in a series on the topic.
plos-pone-0009695:
Fungi grip the surfaces they grow on with sticky proteins called adhesins. Jayashree Ramana and Dinesh Gupta built a computer tool that predicts those proteins from sequence data alone. They presented the method, called FaaPred, in PLOS ONE in 2010.

FaaPred uses a support vector machine, a learning program trained on known examples. It scans a protein's sequence and judges whether it looks like an adhesin. Spotting these glue proteins matters because fungi use them to colonize hosts and surfaces. A fast prediction tool saves lab time by narrowing the list for testing.
plos-pone-0009895:
Southwest China is home to many ethnic minority groups with deep local roots. Hongbin Lin and colleagues read their genetic relationships using shared markers in DNA. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The region borders several countries and mixes many cultures.

The markers are microsatellites, short DNA stretches repeated a variable number of times. Counting repeats shows which groups share closer ancestry. Such maps test stories told by history and language against hard data. They also help protect the genetic heritage of minority peoples. The groups studied live across a wide and rugged region.
plos-pone-0010095:
The authors were Beth Polidoro, Kent Carpenter, Lorna Collins, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study assessed extinction risk for the world's mangrove species. Mangroves are trees adapted to tropical and subtropical coasts. Though few in species number, their forests give services worth billions each year and support coastal livelihoods.

Even so, mangrove areas keep shrinking worldwide. The team mapped which species face the greatest risk and where concern should focus. That geographic view helps conservation groups spend limited money where loss would hurt most. The assessment appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010, with maps of the areas of concern.
plos-pone-0010195:
The authors were Mary Wines-Samuelson, Eva Schulte, Miriam Smith, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mutant mice to model Alzheimer's related brain loss. Presenilin genes are the major known cause of inherited Alzheimer's disease. The team's earlier work showed presenilins are essential for memory and for keeping neurons alive in adult brains.

In mice with presenilins switched off in the cortex, they tracked neuronal degeneration over age. The loss was progressive and age-dependent, worsening as animals grew older. That pattern mirrors human disease timing and gives researchers a model for testing protective ideas.
plos-pone-0010395:
Melissa Naylor and colleagues presented a statistics method for finding gene-control variants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some DNA variants change how much a gene is used, not the protein it makes. Finding those variants links genetics to disease mechanisms. Usual tests check one variant against one gene at a time. That piecemeal approach can miss joint patterns.

Their method, canonical correlation analysis, compares sets of variants with sets of gene readings at once. Looking at both sides as groups can expose links single tests overlook. Better variant maps guide labs toward the genes that truly matter in disease. The paper is a tool for geneticists facing huge data tables. It promises fewer false leads and stronger ones.
plos-pone-0010495:
Ana González and colleagues linked barley's defense genes to resistance against rusts and mildew in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants carry a large family of peroxidase genes, enzymes tied to defense chemistry. Peroxidases rise during disease attack, and their presence varies with resistance. The team profiled these genes across barley lines. They then matched gene clusters to broad resistance against fungal diseases.

Genetic linkage means breeders can select for the protective clusters with DNA markers. Resistance that works against several fungi at once is especially valuable. Barley is a major crop for food, feed, and brewing. Durable disease resistance cuts fungicide use and yield losses. This study gives breeders a genetic map toward that goal.
plos-pone-0010595:
Timothy Read and colleagues sped up a standard bacterial fingerprinting method, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multi-locus sequence typing identifies strains by reading several housekeeping genes. The classic version is accurate but slow, taking days of lab work.

The team moved the method onto tiny fluid-handling chips. The chips ran the same gene reads much faster and with smaller samples. Results matched the slower standard approach. Faster typing could help hospitals and food safety labs spot outbreak strains sooner, while there is still time to act and stop wider spread.
plos-pone-0010695:
Lauren MacNeil and colleagues scanned gene activity after muscle-damaging exercise, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lowering a heavy weight slowly, called eccentric exercise, tears muscle fibers slightly. The muscle then repairs and grows. Female hormone levels were thought to shape that response.

Gene scans after such exercise showed growth pathways switching on in a new pattern. The pattern did not track hormone shifts as expected. Muscle seemed to run its repair program on its own schedule. Athletes and doctors both care about that program, since the same damage-and-repair cycle underlies strength training and recovery from injury.
plos-pone-0010895:
Ramaswamy Sharma, Masahiro Tsuchiya, Ziedonis Skobe and co-authors published this dental study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Too much fluoride can stain and weaken tooth enamel, and the enamel-forming cells called ameloblasts are oddly sensitive to it. The authors proposed that acidity is the missing factor, because the cell's surroundings turn acidic while enamel hardens.

They treated enamel-forming cells with fluoride at neutral and low acidity and tracked stress signals and protein release. At low pH, far smaller fluoride doses switched on stress pathways and disrupted cell function. Sharma and colleagues argue that acid lets fluoride slip into cells more easily, lowering the harm threshold. Their acid test reframes fluorosis risk: the same dose may be safer or riskier depending on the chemistry around the cells.
plos-pone-0010995:
Susie Lee, Lawrence Donehower, Alan Herron and co-authors published this cancer and body clock study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell division in fast-renewing tissues follows a daily rhythm, and shift workers with broken rhythms show higher cancer rates. Mice lacking clock genes develop more tumors, but how a broken clock outside the cell itself could drive cancer was unclear.

The team compared mice missing various clock gene pairs and found all showed more spontaneous and radiation-induced tumors. Tumor growth in clock-mutant cells depended not on the cells alone but on outside growth signals. Among the clock's output pathways, the daily rhythm of sympathetic nerve signaling stood out as a controller of those signals. Lee and colleagues argue that losing daily control of nerve chemistry creates a body-wide climate favoring tumors.
plos-pone-0011095:
Starkey, Zhao, Sadygov and colleagues described kidney research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied diabetic mice and looked at how the kidneys handle a form of vitamin A. To track it, they used heavy oxygen labels and a two step method that separates and weighs molecules.

The team found that the handling of this vitamin A form was altered in diabetic kidneys. Changed chemistry of this kind may mark early kidney damage. It could also affect genes that the vitamin form normally controls. The findings give researchers new leads for markers that catch kidney trouble before it grows severe.
plos-pone-0011195:
Buglino and Resh pinpointed a tagging enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. A key growth signal, named Sonic hedgehog after a game character, cannot work until a fatty tag is attached. The team found which conserved parts of the tagging enzyme are critical for adding that tag.

Without the tag, the signal cannot spread or act properly in a growing embryo. The same signal can also drive some cancers when it stays on in adults. That makes the tagging step a target for cancer drugs. The study marks the exact regions drug designers should aim at.
plos-pone-0011295:
Borkow, Zhou, Page and colleagues tested a germ killing mask in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their face mask contains copper oxide, a material toxic to many viruses. The team checked whether the mask inactivates influenza A virus that lands on it, instead of letting it linger on the surface.

The copper containing mask did show anti influenza activity in their tests. A self disinfecting mask lowers risk for health workers who handle used masks. It could also slow spread in pandemics when masks are worn widely. The technology adds active protection to the simple barrier a normal mask provides.
plos-pone-0011395:
Kari Saikkonen, Piippa Wäli, and Marjo Helander tested in 2010 what decides whether a fungus and a grass can live together. Many grasses host fungi that grow inside their leaves without visible harm, and the fungi can protect the grass from insects and drought. Farmers would like to use that protection, but pairings often fail for no obvious reason.

By crossing different fungus strains with different grass lines, the team found that genetic fit between the partners decides whether the pairing takes hold. Good matches established stable partnerships, while poor matches failed early. That rule has direct farming value. Breeding programs can screen for compatible pairs in advance instead of planting mixtures that quietly fail, and ecologists gain a clearer account of how these hidden partnerships form in wild grasslands.
plos-pone-0011495:
Pauline Chaste and co-authors catalogued in 2010 faulty variants of the melatonin receptors in people with autism and in the general population. Melatonin governs sleep timing, and sleep problems are common in autism spectrum disorders. Receptors for melatonin can carry mutations that bias which signaling path they favor, or that damage the receptor outright, and the team hunted for both kinds.

They identified pathway-biased and harmful receptor mutants across their samples, showing such variants circulate beyond autism as well. Cataloguing them tests whether sleep-hormone wiring contributes to autism biology or mainly to its sleep troubles. Either answer is useful: a real link would open a new research direction, while a clean separation would stop a tempting but false lead. The catalogue itself becomes a reference for any later study of melatonin and the brain.
plos-pone-0011595:
Jennifer Frost and co-authors tested gene imprinting in human placental stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Imprinted genes are used from only one parent's copy, and the largest known cluster sits around the KCNQ1 gene. In that cluster, some genes are imprinted in both mice and humans, while others differ between the two species.

The team checked three genes near the cluster ends, plus the decorin gene, in human trophoblast stem cells. None of the three showed imprinted use in these cells. The result sharpens the map of which genes carry a parent-of-origin stamp in early human development.
plos-pone-0011695:
David de Lima Morais and Paul Harrison compared RNA quality control across mammals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes can be spliced in alternative ways, changing what a protein does or where it goes. When splicing is paired with nonsense-mediated decay, the cell can also use the system to control how much of a message survives.

The authors investigated whether candidacy for this decay is conserved at genome scale. They found large-scale evidence that it is shared across mammals. A shared system suggests RNA proofreading is an ancient, deeply kept feature of mammalian biology rather than a species-by-species improvisation.
plos-pone-0011795:
Scott Houck and John Clark studied a stress protein that also serves the eye lens, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human alphaB crystallin is a small heat shock protein forming large, varied complexes. It modulates the balance between tubulin and the microtubule rods built from it, through a dynamic mechanism that was poorly understood.

The authors show that constant subunit exchange within the crystallin complex underlies that regulation of microtubule assembly. A shape-shifting helper thus tunes the cell's skeleton. The second job reveals versatility in a protein best known for keeping the lens clear.
plos-pone-0011895:
Gerald Gartlehner and co-authors published in 2010 an umbrella review, a review of reviews, on whether medicines work differently in men and women. Sex shapes disease risk, illness patterns, and life span, and scattered studies had reported sex differences in drug benefit and harm. No broad map of that evidence existed.

Gathering systematic reviews across treatments, the team assessed where efficacy and safety genuinely differ by sex and where claims rest on thin data. Their synthesis supports dosing and prescribing that treat sex as a real variable rather than a footnote. It also exposes how often trials still fail to report results separately for women and men.
plos-pone-0011995:
Barney Graham and a large team reported in 2010 a setback for an early HIV vaccine design. The vaccine mixed B and T cell targets from four subtype B HIV strains, delivered as peptides in an oily adjuvant. Healthy, low-risk adult volunteers received it to test safety and immune response.

The mixture was immunogenic, meaning it did provoke immune responses, but it also caused sterile abscesses at injection sites and unacceptable reactogenicity. A vaccine people cannot tolerate cannot be used, however good the lab numbers look. The report closes that formulation's path and warns vaccine makers that this adjuvant pairing carries a real cost in volunteers.
plos-pone-0012095:
Steen Villumsen, Rebecca Pedersen, Karen Krogfelt, and co-authors improved a lab test for leptospirosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease spreads from animals to people, is common in much of the world, and is often missed. Its signs can look like flu at first, yet it can also move on to organ failure, so a fast and sure test matters a great deal.

Blood tests that read the germ's DNA can confirm the disease, but only if enough clean DNA can be pulled from a blood sample. The team refined that extraction step using blood cultures, making the DNA test more reliable. A better test helps doctors start the right treatment sooner, before mild illness turns severe.
plos-pone-0012195:
Benjamin Pitcher, Robert Harcourt, and Isabelle Charrier studied how fast sea lion mothers and pups learn each other's voices, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Australian sea lions raise pups in crowded colonies where a mother returning from the sea must find her own pup among hundreds. Voice recognition solves that problem, but how soon after birth it works, and which side learns first, varies between species.

Their tests show the recognition develops remarkably fast on this breeding colony. Missing the window would cost a pup its meals, so speed is survival. The work adds a case to the science of animal communication, and it helps wildlife carers judge how disturbance at colonies affects the youngest animals.
plos-pone-0012295:
Michael Zaragoza, Joseph Fass, Marta Diegoli, and co-authors hunted mitochondrial DNA variants in heart muscle diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mitochondria carry their own small genome, passed only from mother to child, and its mutations can cause inherited heart failure. A complication is mixture: a person can carry some normal and some mutated copies, and the proportions shape how sick they become.

Using next-generation sequencing, which reads DNA at great depth, the team discovered and evaluated variants in patients with cardiomyopathy. Deep reading can spot low-level mixtures older tests missed. Better variant catalogs turn a confusing genetic test into guidance a family can act on.
plos-pone-0012395:
Juan García-Arriaza, José Nájera, Carmen Gómez and co-workers profiled an HIV vaccine candidate in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The candidate, MVA-B, uses a weakened poxvirus to carry four HIV proteins into the body. Which immune responses a vaccine must raise to block HIV is still unknown, so careful profiling of each candidate matters before human trials.

The team measured the strength and type of mouse immune responses and tested whether deleting certain virus genes made responses stronger. The deletions did boost key responses. Profiling of this kind helps vaccine designers pick the best version to carry forward, a slow but vital step toward an effective HIV vaccine.
plos-pone-0012495:
Xianfu Yi, Yu-Dong Cai, Zhisong He and colleagues predicted where DNA spools sit along the genome, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Eukaryotic DNA wraps around histone spools called nucleosomes, and their positions decide which genes are open for use. The authors tested whether the binding sites of gene switch proteins can forecast those positions.

Their predictor uses the pattern of transcription factor binding sites to place nucleosomes along a sequence. Where switches gather, spools tend to give way. A good forecast helps researchers read new genomes and understand how cells keep needed genes reachable while packing away the rest into tight chromatin.
plos-pone-0012595:
Laxman, Sutter and Tu published a yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject is the yeast metabolic cycle, a rhythm in which growing yeast cells swing between high and low oxygen use. Most work on that rhythm had tracked whole cultures at once. The team instead asked how single cells behave inside a cycling group.

To watch one cell at a time, they used glowing reporter tags tied to genes that switch on and off with the cycle. The films let them see whether each cell keeps time with its neighbours or drifts on its own. That single-cell view helps explain how a whole culture can pulse in step.
plos-pone-0012795:
Hernandez-Martinez, Navarro-Cerrillo, Caccia and co-authors studied a moth that no longer fears the main biological pesticide. Bacillus thuringiensis, or Bt, is the most used microbe for killing crop pests. The beet armyworm Spodoptera exigua has evolved resistance, threatening that tool's future.

Their 2010 study found the resistant moths keep their gut defence response against Bt switched on all the time. A defence that never sleeps may carry costs elsewhere in the insect's life. Knowing the trick helps design ways to slow or undo resistance.  Gut responses were compared between resistant and normal moths directly.
plos-pone-0331995:
Mathew Kipsum and colleagues field-tested a new mosquito net that stacks three defences against malaria in western Kenya. Standard nets rely on one insecticide family, and resistant mosquitoes are eroding their value. The 2026 evaluation put the triple net through laboratory assays, tunnel tests, and experimental huts against resistant local mosquitoes.

The net combines a pyrethroid, a growth regulator that sterilises mosquitoes, and a synergist that blocks detox enzymes. In laboratory assays it killed about nineteen of twenty mosquitoes and stopped a similar share from feeding, across repeated washes. Judged against two rival dual nets and a standard net, it met the study's comparison bars. Kipsum and colleagues add evidence for multi-ingredient nets where resistance bites.
plos-pone-0335995:
The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill harmed Gulf Coast families in many ways. Mothers lost jobs, income, and daily stability. Ariane Lisann Rung and colleagues asked whether those losses hurt children's mental health. Their study covered about four hundred forty-five mother and child pairs. All lived in Louisiana. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Oil exposure alone showed no direct link to child outcomes. But harder-hit mothers reported greater loss of resources. Greater loss then went with worse mental health scores in their children. The children averaged about thirteen years old. The authors draw a practical lesson. Disaster aid that restores household resources may shield children indirectly.
plos-pone-0336195:
Michael Agyemang Kwarteng, Ngozika Esther Ezinne, and co-authors surveyed optometry students across ten Nigerian universities about anxiety, depression, and stress, using a standard twenty-one-item screening scale. Their 2026 web survey drew four hundred seventy-four students, mostly in their early twenties, and linked symptom levels to background factors.

Half the students reported depressive symptoms, and about fifteen percent rated them severe or worse. Severe anxiety affected more than a third, and a quarter carried all three conditions at once. Nearly half had at least two overlapping problems. Women faced significantly higher odds of depression and of overall distress than men. The authors urge structured mental health support and prevention inside optometry training programs, arguing the burden is too large to treat as private struggle.
plos-pone-0338995:
Lanchuan Zhang and co-authors surveyed outdoor workers in Chengdu, China, about suboptimal health, the grey zone between feeling well and being ill. Drivers, construction workers, security guards, and couriers spend long days exposed to weather and strain, yet their in-between health complaints rarely reach doctors. The team used a standard sub-health scale on just over seven hundred valid responses.

Four in five workers showed some degree of sub-health, a strikingly high share. Drivers fared worst, then guards, builders, and finally couriers. Age, years spent working outdoors, marital status, family size, income, drinking, and regular exercise all connected with the condition. The authors call for measures aimed at these drivers of decline, arguing that catching workers in the grey zone is cheaper than treating full illness later.
plos-pone-0341995:
Youjin Lee and colleagues present a computer method for spotting early cognitive decline from brain scans, in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. They used a type of PET scan that shows how the brain uses sugar, a signal that weakens as Alzheimer's disease develops. Their approach feeds the scan into the model at two scales at once: fine detail across the whole brain, and average values for set regions.

Trained on scans from a large Alzheimer's research programme, the combined model sorted people with decline from healthy peers more accurately than either scale alone. Sensitivity to real decline improved the most. Better scan reading could support earlier diagnosis, when treatment and planning help most.
plos-pone-0344395:
Victor Luckyboy Dzramado, Obed U. Lasim, and Emmanuel Oduro turn research on HIV treatment in Ghana into a set of policy proposals. Sticking with daily antiretroviral drugs keeps the virus down, yet many patients miss doses. Their 2026 article builds on a large mixed-methods study of two thousand patients in the Ashanti Region and the barriers they face.

The authors propose four structural fixes rather than more lectures to patients. Travel support would cut missed visits, community refill points would ease drug access, clinics could trim waits and protect privacy, and income plus food support would tackle poverty barriers. Each proposal is framed as a testable bet for officials working with tight budgets.
plos-pone-0344895:
Raquel V Oliveira and Elizabeth Culatta followed more than thirteen hundred young people with heavy justice-system contact, asking how different kinds of contact relate to mental health. Their 2026 PLOS One paper uses a long-running American study that tracked these youths across ten waves from 2000 to 2010.

Arrests and stays in institutions lined up with more anxiety, depression, hostility, and unusual thoughts at the same point in time. Court appearances, a milder contact, lined up with symptoms that grew later instead. Drug use and crime involvement tracked with symptoms throughout. The authors say even light contact can act as a lasting stressor for young people.
plos-pone-0345895:
Caizhen Chen and Xiuguo Zhang studied whether a common blood protein can warn of leg vein clots before hip fracture surgery. Their patients were all aged eighty or over with a break between the hip and thigh bone. The 2026 study reviewed records for close to fifteen hundred such patients admitted over eight years.

Patients with lower albumin, the protein measured, had more clots found before surgery. Each step up in albumin came with slightly lower odds of a clot, and the pattern was steady rather than curved. The link held in most patient subgroups and in checks designed to test its strength. Chen and Zhang say albumin may help flag patients who need the closest clot watch, pending further study.
plos-pone-0346095:
Yi Huang and colleagues compared the blood health of Yangtze finless porpoises living in two parts of Poyang Lake, China's largest freshwater lake. These endangered river porpoises were examined at two sites holding nineteen and six animals, with blood counts and chemistry set against known healthy ranges. Statistical methods teased apart which differences truly belonged to the habitat rather than to individual quirks.

Porpoises at the Piaotou site looked healthier overall, with stronger oxygen-carrying capacity, better nutrition markers, and livelier metabolism. The Jinxi Lake animals showed signs of clotting activation or inflammation, very low counts of one white cell type, and more values straying outside healthy ranges. The authors use the contrast to argue that conservation for this species must be habitat-specific, since one lake holds pockets of very different living conditions.
plos-pone-0346695:
Evie A Malaia and co-authors recorded brain waves from Deaf adults who sign in Austrian Sign Language while they watched videos of signing and of other human movement. The team asked how a lifetime of using a visual language, and simple ageing, reshape the brain's habit of predicting what comes next. That habit is well studied in hearing people but little explored in the visual channel.

Older and more experienced signers showed brain responses that locked more tightly onto the flow of linguistic movement, with shifts in signal complexity over the front and sides of the head. Experience, in other words, keeps refining prediction rather than letting it fade. The authors say language leaves its mark on prediction through whichever sense carries it, hearing or sight.
plos-pone-0346995:
Rasha Alkholy, Penny Bee, Rebecca Pedley, and Karina Lovell wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports a qualitative study carried out in the United Kingdom with older adults from varied cultural backgrounds. The topic is what these adults believe helps them cope when they feel anxious.

The study is guided by a framework from Leventhal about how people make sense of a health problem and manage their own response to it. Through participants' own accounts, the authors examine which coping strategies older adults trust and why. The findings speak to clinicians and service planners who support mental health in later life across mixed communities.
plos-pone-0347495:
Antonis Koutsoumpis and colleagues ran a cross-cultural test of a fashion myth: that horizontal stripes make the wearer look wider. In fact, laboratory vision studies find striped figures judged slimmer. Across Greece, the Netherlands, and Taiwan, the team's 2026 experiments first confirmed that people everywhere believe stripes widen, then asked them to judge dresses in a perception task.

The striped dress was again seen as thinner than a plain one of equal width. Belief and perception interacted lopsidedly: people who believed stripes slim saw the dress as slimmer still, while believers in the widening myth showed no matching distortion. The asymmetry held across all three countries, suggesting a universal quirk of vision and belief.
plos-pone-0347595:
Hideki Kawai and colleagues asked whether heart scans taken a year or more into treatment can warn of future trouble in cardiac sarcoidosis, a condition where inflammatory clusters damage the heart. Seventy-nine patients on immune-suppressing therapy had sugar-based tracer scans, which light up where heart tissue is inflamed and hungry. The team then tracked deaths, dangerous rhythms, device shocks, and heart failure admissions.

Patients whose scans still showed uptake suffered more major events over the following two years, although the signal weakened in adjusted models and over longer horizons. Among patients whose hearts still pumped strongly, event rates stayed low regardless of scan results, and repeat scans showed inflammation usually cooling on treatment. The authors see the scan as one useful clue among several, strongest when combined with pumping function.
plos-pone-0347695:
Preeclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy, can worsen fast, and few treatments slow it. Kehinde S Okunade and colleagues present a trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing whether a common antioxidant drug can delay that worsening in Lagos, Nigeria.

About one hundred fifty women diagnosed early, between roughly six and eight months of pregnancy, will take a daily tablet of the drug or a look-alike placebo alongside normal care. Neither patients nor staff will know who gets which. The main measure is how many days pass before the disease advances. Results are not yet available; the trial runs through 2028.
plos-pone-0348195:
Haoge Shou and colleagues tested how adding yttrium, a rare earth metal, changes magnesium under repeated uneven loading. Light magnesium alloys suit cars and aircraft, yet they slowly stretch out of shape under cycles, a flaw called ratcheting. Pure magnesium and a magnesium yttrium alloy were cycled and then examined under electron microscopes.

Pure magnesium was stronger in a single pull, but the alloy resisted cycle drift far better. It hardened as cycles ran and lasted much longer before failing. Microscopy showed dense tangles of a hard to trigger slip type in the alloy, spreading strain evenly. Alloy designers can borrow that trick to build lighter parts that hold shape under vibration.
plos-pone-0348495:
Shinya Kato, Akihiro Yoshida, and co-authors tested a compound from licorice root against dental plaque, comparing it with a common antiseptic used in mouthwashes. The licorice compound was already known to kill plaque bacteria and slow new biofilm growth, but its effect on plaque already formed was untested. Their 2026 lab study grew plaque biofilms for a day, then applied each agent and counted living and dead bacteria.

The licorice treatment cut the number of living bacteria versus a control solvent. More unusually, it loosened the biofilm itself: the liquid above treated samples turned cloudiest, showing the most shed material, well beyond the antiseptic. The authors suggest the compound strips plaque off surfaces by a route different from simple killing, which could help prevent gum disease.
plos-pone-0348595:
Ferozkhan Jadhakhan, Deborah Falla, and Alexander Dallaway follow adults hospitalized after bone and muscle injuries to see who develops lasting post-traumatic stress symptoms. Such symptoms hamper recovery and quality of life. Their 2026 study reanalyzes a cohort of one hundred twenty-five patients at a British major trauma center, measuring symptoms just after injury and again at three and six months.

Nearly everyone crossed the symptom threshold in the raw first days, a figure the authors tie to the early timing and sensitive cut-off. By three months about a quarter still qualified, and fewer by six. Road crashes raised the risk compared with falls. Oddly, higher early anxiety and fear of movement linked with lower later risk in the models, inviting closer study of early coping.
plos-pone-0348695:
Lucas Praetzel and colleagues ran a small pilot study on a trick to make prostate cancer easier to see on scans. The scans rely on a protein called PSMA, which sits on prostate cells but is sometimes too scarce to detect. Earlier lab work suggested the drug dutasteride can raise PSMA levels. Four patients in this 2026 study took the drug for one week between two scans.

Signal strength rose in every patient after the drug course. Biopsies then confirmed cancer in the brightened spots, while one spot that faded proved cancer-free. With only four patients, the authors call the result a promising lead: a short drug course before scanning might catch tumours that would otherwise stay hidden.
plos-pone-0348895:
Haoran Zhu and colleagues present HBGCN, a neural network that predicts which drugs will act on which proteins, the first step in finding new medicines and new uses for old ones. Testing every drug against every target in a laboratory is impossible, so prediction narrows the field. Their network learns from a web of mixed biological entities, drugs, proteins, genes, and their relationships, passing messages along both direct and indirect paths.

On benchmark datasets the model performed competitively with leading methods. Case studies showed it surfacing plausible treatment candidates and highlighting the proteins and gene patterns behind its predictions. Predictions that come with a mechanism attached are far more useful to drug hunters than bare scores, because they suggest the experiments to run next.
plos-pone-0349295:
Sofia Kouki and colleagues tested whether machine-assisted image analysis can describe the grains inside archaeological mudbricks as reliably as a human expert. Mudbrick has been a building material since the first farming villages, and grain size and shape reveal how builders chose and prepared their mud. The standard expert method, counting points under a microscope, is slow and varies between analysts.

Their workflow uses a clustering algorithm on microscope images to extract grain size, sorting, and shape automatically. They applied it to forty-five images from two distant sites: Artaxata in Armenia and Los Villares in Spain. Faster, repeatable measurement would let archaeologists compare building traditions across regions without years of microscope work by specialists.
plos-pone-0349395:
Cong Hien Dinh and Anh Vu Le led a plan for a robot that cleans aircraft cabins. Planes turn around fast between flights, so cleaning must be quick. Cabins are tight and oddly shaped. Normal cleaning robots do not fit well. This robot can change its own shape. The 2026 plan splits the work into two stages.

First, the robot cleans open areas like aisles at full size. It skips the seat rows. Then it shrinks and cleans the tight spots it skipped. A search method based on evolution picks the best order of visits. It also counts the energy cost of each shape change. In tests based on real cabins, the plan beat standard methods on both time and energy.
plos-pone-0349595:
Road agencies must budget upkeep before damage forces costly rebuilds, and Chunyan Jia and colleagues forecast those preventive costs for expressways in Xinjiang, China. Their 2026 PLOS One study built a separate tuned model for each of three treatments: filling cracks, sealing surfaces, and laying new overlay.

Each model pairs a proven predictor with a nature-inspired tuning search: fruit fly, hiking, and swarm methods respectively. Tuning lifted accuracy notably in each case, with the crack-filling model explaining most cost variation. The authors argue one general model blurs real differences between treatments, and agencies should forecast each treatment on its own terms.
plos-pone-0349795:
Zac Tran and colleagues asked whether liver transplant patients who receive truly enormous amounts of fluid and blood face worse survival than those receiving merely massive amounts. Liver transplants often bleed heavily, and twenty liters or more marks an extreme group. The single-center study matched patients on recipient, donor, and operative traits so the comparison was fair.

Records from 2009 to 2023 covered adults whose total fluid around surgery reached at least ten liters. Outcomes included deaths at ninety days, at three years, and overall. Knowing whether the extreme-volume group carries extra risk beyond illness severity helps teams judge prognosis and plan intensive care. Such patients form a distinct, fragile group in transplant practice.
plos-pone-0349895:
Tomoko Matsumoto and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study tracking exclusionary nationalism in prewar Japan through newspaper language. Their marker is how readily Japanese newspapers accepted or rejected foreign loanwords, a quiet signal of openness toward outsiders. The team analyzed more than three hundred thousand articles published between 1912 and 1943 and applied a change-point method to find when attitudes shifted.

The signal of exclusionary nationalism appeared in 1936 and then swung up and down rather than climbing steadily toward the Pacific War. Attitudes distinguishing future enemies from allies were already visible in the 1920s. The authors offer the loanword approach as a quantitative way to date and size nationalist turns in other countries and periods.
plos-pone-0350095:
Ja-Ho Koo and Dimitri P Solomatine led a study of flood planning for dams. Forecast tools spawn thousands of paths a river might take. No team can plan for them all. So the set must shrink, but stay true. The team grew paths with a learning model that states its own doubt. Then they tried four ways to prune the set.

The model caught the flow's rhythm and scored well short-term. It still missed peak floods, for lack of past data. One pruning method, based on energy distance, kept the set's stats most true. Plain distance methods kept the wild flood paths best. Those paths matter most for safety. The team lays out the trade-offs for dam crews.
plos-pone-0350295:
Noelia Rodríguez-Blanco and colleagues surveyed nursing students in the province of Alicante, Spain, about adult vaccination. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2026, asked what students knew about the national adult vaccine schedule and how they felt about recommending vaccines. More than five hundred students from three universities answered the survey in spring 2025.

Nearly four in ten students did not know the adult vaccination schedule, though knowledge improved in later years of the degree. Attitudes toward vaccination were mostly positive, and many students said they would recommend vaccines to patients. The gap between goodwill and knowledge points to a clear fix in how nursing courses teach adult immunization.
plos-pone-0350395:
Can Guo, Tang Liu, and their co-authors studied whether physical weakness in older adults raises the risk of osteomyelitis, a serious bone infection. Their 2026 study used health records from the UK Biobank, a large British health database that followed hundreds of thousands of adults. They compared people who later developed the infection with similar people who did not.

Weakness was scored with five simple signs, including slow walking and a weak grip. People classed as pre-frail had clearly higher odds of bone infection, and those classed as frail had odds close to three times higher. The risk rose step by step across the groups. The results suggest that spotting frailty early could help doctors protect patients from a hard-to-treat infection.
plos-pone-0350495:
Akinori Tawaraya and Atsushi Keyaki studied older patients in hospital with aspiration pneumonia, where food or fluid slips into the lungs. Early checks of swallowing and early return to eating by mouth can aid recovery, yet timing varies. A new pathway tightened teamwork between doctors and speech therapists to make those calls faster and more alike.

Three hundred patients aged sixty five and older were compared, with and without the pathway. Patients on the pathway had close to four times the odds of eating by mouth within two days. Late swallowing checks cut those odds. Early eating showed no clear rise in harms like longer stays or repeat pneumonia in early checks.
plos-pone-0350695:
Takuya Hidaka and co-authors in Japan reported a new laboratory method in 2026 for watching a key cell signal inside single cells. The signal is phosphorylation, a small chemical tag that switches proteins on or off, and it is usually too scarce to measure one cell at a time.

Their system labels the proteins of one cell, pulls out the tagged ones with antibodies, and reads them with a custom microscope that can spot single molecules. Tested on human cells treated with a drug, it showed that cells differed widely from each other in ways that bulk tests hide. Such detail could help explain why cell signals vary so much.
plos-pone-0350895:
Yunjing Li and colleagues tested whether steady general-practice care helps older patients who live with both type two diabetes and heart or vessel disease. Two hundred patients leaving a hospital in Qinhuangdao, China, were split by chance into two groups. One got personal health teaching, community follow-up visits, and lifestyle coaching for a year; the other got routine discharge advice.

After a year, the managed group had stayed on its recommended medicines, while the routine group had let several slip. Smoking fell only in the managed group, and its members ate better and moved more. Blood sugar and cholesterol improved in both groups, but the managed patients held wider clinical gains. The trial supports ongoing primary care over one-time advice for this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0351295:
Sisi Zhuang and Lili Zuo compared blood chemistry in children with sepsis, a severe response to infection that can harm many organs. Using a public data set, they contrasted cases caused by bacteria with cases caused by viruses, and with healthy children. Their tools sorted hundreds of small molecules found in blood serum.

Fourteen molecules stood out between the groups, mostly tied to how the body handles nitrogen and a few key building blocks for proteins. Three of them, choline, glutamate, and glutamine, separated bacterial cases from viral cases especially well. Computer models built on them sorted cases with high accuracy. If later work confirms them, such markers could help doctors tell the cause sooner and choose treatment faster.
plos-pone-0351395:
Ivaneliza Simionato de Assis and colleagues surveyed more than four hundred nurses in primary care in Parana state, Brazil, about follow up care for babies born early. Early birth affects about one in ten births worldwide and drives deaths in young children. A standard tool scored five areas, from hospital discharge planning to family support, and maps showed how scores varied by place.

Discharge planning scored worst, with most ratings judged inadequate. Family support scored best, with most ratings good. Home visits, child health checks, and links between services sat in between. Nurses see family care as a strength to build on, while the handoff from hospital to clinic needs urgent repair.
plos-pone-0351495:
Rie Shimoju studied a brain relay point for touch in male rats, and how it shapes seeking a pleasant stroke. Gentle rhythmic stroking makes rats call with high happy sounds and come back for more. A calming drug was placed into the relay, which takes touch signals from the spine toward higher brain areas, to quiet it for a short time.

With the relay quieted, rats stopped approaching for the reward, yet their happy calls during stroking barely changed. Basic feeling and movement stayed intact. Seeking and feeling thus split apart in the brain: the relay seems needed to act on wanting touch, but not to voice pleasure once touch arrives.
plos-pone-0352095:
Pokushalov and colleagues, in a 2026 trial, test whether a group therapy program can lower the body's stress hormones. Long-term stress strains the system that releases cortisol, the main stress hormone, yet trials rarely measure it richly. Their program mixes social and emotional skills training, slow breathing with biofeedback, and reframing of stressful thoughts.

Sixty adults were assigned at random to the eight-week program or to an active comparison program of equal length. Stress output was measured from saliva collected across three days, and from hair, which stores a month-by-month record. The therapy group cut daily cortisol output far more than the control group, and the gain held at six months. Related measures, including a second stress chemical in saliva and hair cortisol, also fell further. The authors say the study shows talk and breathing work can leave a measurable mark on body chemistry.
plos-pone-0352395:
Pongkwan Yimsaard and seven colleagues study cannabis and sexual health among young Bangkok clinic visitors. Their 2026 mixed-method study follows Thailand's cannabis decriminalisation. Two hundred adults aged eighteen to twenty-four at sexual health clinics run by key-population groups completed surveys. Records added laboratory results for HIV and other infections. Fifteen cannabis users and fifteen non-users sat for deep interviews. The clinics serve groups at HIV risk, including gay men and transgender women.

About twenty-two percent of participants had used cannabis in the last month. Statistical tests then linked use patterns with sexual and prevention behaviours. Interview themes added the reasoning behind the numbers: how users see cannabis affecting desire, caution, and condom or medication use. Evidence of this kind was scarce for the new policy era. It gives Thai health services a grounded picture of where cannabis, sex, and HIV prevention actually intersect for young people.
plos-pone-0352995:
