Eunju Jang, Ki Yoon Moon, and Sang Seob Yun ask a pointed question. Do years on dialysis before a kidney transplant shadow the years after it? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It used records from South Korea. They followed more than eighteen hundred first-time recipients. The patients were treated between 2006 and 2021. Each was sorted by how long dialysis had lasted before surgery. One group had never dialysed at all.

Patients in the longest-dialysis group died at notably higher rates. Their dialysis had averaged close to nine years. Those transplanted early fared better. The link with losing the new kidney was weaker. It was also inconsistent, especially for deceased-donor organs. The message for waiting-list policy is plain. Time on dialysis is not neutral, and earlier transplantation saves lives.
plos-pone-0353195:
Hiratsuka and colleagues built a simple branching model in a 2026 study to estimate which patients with advanced cancer live at least a year. Patients well enough to attend clinics face hard choices about care, and most older tools predict only weeks or months ahead. The team drew on a Korean group study of two hundred patients whom doctors expected to live a year or less.

Three easy-to-get measures split patients into four groups with different outlooks. The model matched real outcomes closely in repeat testing. Average survival in the group was well under a year, which underlines the stakes. After checks in other settings, such a short tool could help doctors raise care planning talks at the right time.
plos-pone-0353295:
Querino da Silva and colleagues reviewed new marker candidates for bowel inflammation diseases in a 2026 paper. Crohn's disease and related conditions are hard to diagnose and manage because standard tests can miss activity and patients respond unevenly to drugs. The review gathered work from five databases on gene, protein, and microbe markers plus imaging and sensor tools.

Candidate markers were sorted by use: early diagnosis, tracking activity, forecasting course, and predicting drug response. Artificial intelligence tools that combine many signals drew special attention. The authors frame these markers as steps toward care matched to each patient, while noting that most candidates still need strong proof in clinics before routine use.
plos-pone-0353395:
Mohammad Najeh Samara and three colleagues ask leaders at a veterans' nursing home in New York what makes recreational therapy succeed or stall, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Nineteen senior staff completed a detailed survey mixing scores with written answers. Recreational programmes — exercise, arts, group activities — are central to wellbeing for ageing veterans, yet their organisational supports are rarely examined.

Leaders rated the programme effective overall, with physical wellbeing the strongest gain, and praised the variety of activities above all. The glaring weakness was resources: a capacity index under thirty percent signalled critical strain. Engaged residents and committed staff rose together in the ratings. The authors offer their analysis as a planning tool for administrators.
plos-pone-0353695:
Shao, Gong, and Shen tested two blood ratios as warning signs in severe pneumonia in a 2026 study. Records covered nearly two hundred adults treated at one Chinese hospital over three years. Both ratios combine routine lab values tied to inflammation and nutrition, so they cost nothing extra to compute.

Patients who died had higher values of the first ratio than survivors. People below the chosen cutoffs for either ratio survived at much higher rates over their hospital stay. The first ratio predicted death more accurately than the second. Simple ratios like these could help doctors spot high-risk pneumonia patients early, when closer watch matters most.
plos-pone-0354595:
Aina Li and co-authors search in 2026 for genes that link kidney stones to vessel lining failure, a step toward hardened arteries. People with kidney stones face higher risk of vessel disease, but shared mechanisms were unclear. Three public datasets were mined for genes changed in both conditions, then a shrinking regression picked candidate markers and lab checks confirmed expression in stone samples.

Two markers stood out as key, with one clearly overactive in stone tissue. Network work tied them to cell sticking, adhesion, and recycling pathways, plus immune cell patterns. Drug prediction flagged several cancer drugs as possible matches for one marker. Personal treatment ideas remain early.
plos-pone-0354695:
Jiejun Yuan and four colleagues published this 2026 simulation study of tunnel flooding disasters in karst rock. Water flowing through limestone cavities slowly washes out the loose fill inside them, until a sudden inrush can flood a tunnel. Using a particle-based computer method, they varied fill grain size, squeezing stress, and water speed.

Their key signal was a bending point in how fast particles were being lost, which marks the turn toward collapse. Safe warning ranges differed sharply between fine and coarse fills. Yuan's thresholds could help tunnel crews set alarms before erosion crosses into catastrophe.
plos-pone-0354795:
José Rodríguez-Olivares and co-authors test in 2026 how well referral rules and tumour staining pick out Mexican bowel cancer patients who carry inherited risk variants. All such patients should be assessed, since results shape treatment and family testing. Gene panel testing served as the truth standard against which a risk calculator, two clinical rule sets, and protein staining were judged.

About a third of patients carried a harmful variant, most in the classic syndrome genes. One rule set caught almost all carriers but flagged many others, while another was highly specific. The calculator and staining both performed well. Panels testing many genes at once are recommended.
plos-pone-0354895:
Yan Zhang and three colleagues listen to women who are pregnant again after losing a baby, focusing on how they sleep, in this 2026 qualitative study from a hospital in Suzhou, China. Eighteen women in the late stage of pregnancy took part in semi-structured interviews about their nights. Their experiences have rarely been documented, despite the heavy grief and anxiety this group carries.

Three themes emerged. Sleep was often severely disrupted. Many forces fed the problem, from psychological burden and physical discomfort to unhelpful habits, thin support from family and friends, and too little guidance from healthcare providers. Women also struggled to manage the problem on their own. The authors urge providers to screen for physical discomfort and mental strain early, correct unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and build layered support for these mothers.
plos-pone-0355195:
Thaísa Bissoli and co-authors describe every twin birth in Brazil across a decade, using the national live birth registry. Twin pregnancies carry outsized risk, and Brazil's size means regional gaps matter. The analysis linked records into complete twin pairs. There were well over two hundred thousand pairs. Mothers were profiled by age, schooling, care use, and delivery mode. Newborn outcomes included low weight, early birth, and size mismatch within pairs.

Most mothers were in their late twenties or early thirties, had attended many prenatal visits, and delivered by cesarean at a strikingly high rate. Around three in five twins arrived early and underweight, with the heaviest burden in the richer south and southeast, while size mismatch within pairs stayed similar everywhere. Bissoli and colleagues call the pattern a standing challenge for Brazilian maternity care.
plos-pone-0355295:
Kedir Dendir and co-authors measure in 2026 iron shortage anaemia among pregnant women at their first antenatal visit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Women at one health centre answered questions and gave blood for iron store and haemoglobin tests. Globally, iron shortage drives about half of anaemia cases, so local figures guide clinic advice.

Anaemia was uncommon in this group, and iron shortage anaemia rarer still, well below many wider estimates. Thin arm size, eating fewer meals, and eating a narrow range of foods linked strongly to the condition. The authors advise nutrition teaching for mothers and wider community studies to confirm the low rate.
plos-pone-0355395:
Jean Xavier leads a team of seven studying how children take another person's point of view through touch, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mirror letters, b, d, p, and q, were traced on each child's stomach. The signal is ambiguous. It can be read from one's own perspective or from a facing person's. One hundred seven children aged six to seventeen took part, including children with autism or developmental coordination disorder, conditions where visual perspective taking is known to falter.

Left to choose, children in every group read the letters from their viewpoint, at similar rates. When a perspective was imposed, accuracy grew with age for all. The neurodivergent group scored lower in an imposed session, and response times diverged mainly for the decentered view. Touch, it seems, defaults to the self for everyone, and learning to flip that view is a developmental climb rather than a group dividing line.
plos-pone-0355495:
Ahmed M Sayed, Nada M Ezzelarab, and Nguyen Tien Huy compared how cancer and neurology drugs move through United States approval. They asked whether speed comes from stacking fast-track perks or from trial design. Their 2026 study reviewed nearly two hundred original approvals from 2015 to 2024. It scored each drug's bundle of expedited designations. It then examined the trials behind each approval.

Cancer drugs collected more expedited perks. They cleared regulatory review months faster than neurology drugs. Yet total time from development start to approval barely differed. Neurology trials were more often randomized, blinded, and late-stage. Cancer trials often used single groups. The contrast suggests review speed reflects the evidence package regulators accept, not just the perks a sponsor collects.
plos-pone-0355595:
Daiana Colledani and seven colleagues improve a screening tool for hikikomori, the severe and prolonged social withdrawal first described in Japan, in this 2026 study. Data came from a national survey of nearly nine thousand Italian teenagers who completed a fifteen-item questionnaire about withdrawal. The goal was to make the tool faster and more clinically useful without losing accuracy.

The researchers set a cutoff score that best separated at-risk teenagers and identified four distinct profiles that differed in anxiety, depression, impulsivity, and risky behavior. They then built an adaptive version that asks only the questions each person needs, cutting the length roughly in half while reproducing full scores closely. Packaged into an app that handles scoring and reporting, the short test could help schools and clinics spot withdrawn teenagers far earlier.
plos-pone-0355695:
Aqsa Rubab and colleagues produced a full breed profile of the Sipli sheep of Punjab, Pakistan, measuring bodies, wool, milk, reproduction, and growth in a flock at a government breeding center. Their 2026 study weighed and measured eighty-two adults, sampled wool across seasons, analyzed milk from fourteen ewes, and fitted four growth curve models to lamb records from two years.

Rams outmeasured ewes across the board, and male lambs stayed heavier at every age. One growth model, Brody's, described the breed's curve best. Autumn wool ran thicker and ram wool carried more coarse fiber than ewe wool. Pregnancy and lambing data completed the baseline. Such characterization is the necessary first step before any serious breeding or conservation program for a local breed.
plos-pone-0356295:
Dina Lelic and Frederic Marmel set out reference values for how everyday sounds feel to older listeners, in this 2026 study. Hearing researchers use a standard set of recorded sounds, from animal calls to tools and running water, to study emotion and hearing together. Until now, the benchmark ratings came mostly from younger adults, which limits studies of aging.

Ninety people in their middle and later years, all reporting normal hearing, rated each of the sounds online for pleasantness and intensity. Pleasant sounds tended to feel calmer, while unpleasant ones felt more arousing. Surprisingly, age, gender, and self-reported hearing habits did not predict the ratings. The published values now give researchers a fair comparison point when they study emotional responses to sound in older adults, including those with hearing problems.
plos-pone-0356395:
Kelly Carrasco and seven colleagues ran a pilot study in 2026 on a new kind of virtual classroom. Their system uses a green-screen trick to place students inside a recorded, wraparound video of a real lecture hall. The team wanted to know whether such a setup is workable for teaching and research, and how students remember, feel, and physically respond inside it.

Just over one hundred university students watched a prerecorded lecture this way and took tests before and after. Recall improved clearly right after the lecture, though overall scores stayed modest. Students felt moderately present in the virtual room and reported only mild discomfort, and feeling present did not predict better memory. The authors say short sessions like this are a feasible research tool.
plos-pone-0356495:
Oksana Artemchuk and colleagues followed 403 healthcare workers in six Georgian hospitals through three flu seasons, asking who actually takes the annual influenza vaccine they are urged to get. Their 2026 cohort study combined vaccination records with an attitudes survey and modeled which beliefs and traits separated the vaccinated from the never-vaccinated.

Nearly three in ten workers skipped vaccination in all three seasons. Disbelief in the vaccine's safety cut the odds of vaccination by almost three quarters, and doubts about effectiveness cut them deeply too. Workers in their forties were the most likely to vaccinate, and one hospital lagged dramatically. Job type and sex made no difference. The authors advise campaigns that argue safety head-on rather than repeating generic encouragement.
plos-pone-0356695:
Ayaka Uchiyama and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE building a Japanese version of a scale that measures how work and private life blend together. Long hours are routine in Japan, and remote work has blurred the line further, so balancing two separate spheres fits daily life poorly. The team translated an existing work-life integration scale, surveyed more than seven hundred employed adults, and checked the tool's structure, reliability, and stability over time.

The original four-part structure did not fit the Japanese data. Analysis instead supported three parts: interference between work and life, strain between work and family, and ways work and family enrich each other. The scale held up against five established measures of conflict, enrichment, satisfaction, and mental health, and scores stayed fairly steady on retesting. Full-time and part-time workers differed in patterned ways, giving researchers a validated tool for studying Japanese workplaces.
plos-pone-0356895:
Yitian Liu, Zhou Zhao, and Kun Qi built a way to generate cartoon animations with strong, controllable feelings. They used generative AI tools. Two chronic weaknesses drove the work. Feelings often drift off-script, and characters feel generic. Their 2026 study layered prompts in a hierarchy. Each request was encoded along three lines: the feeling, the behavior, and the style. A language model read the request, and a video tool made the images.

Test runs held face, movement rhythm, and color mood in close agreement with the requested feeling. Different user profiles produced visibly different expression sizes, tempos, and styles. That showed the personal touch worked. The layered prompting also improved movement logic and fine gesture detail. The authors offer the scheme as a template for controllable creative AI.
plos-pone-0356995:
Yeoeun Lim and Moonwon Hwang compared three machines that measure the cornea's curve in everyday clinic conditions. They used 227 eyes of cataract surgery candidates. Their 2026 study matters because toric lens implants are chosen from exactly these measurements. Toric lenses correct astigmatism during cataract surgery. Prior device comparisons were run under tidy research conditions.

On average the devices agreed well. For individual patients they often did not. Predicted leftover astigmatism from device disagreements passed the meaningful line in nearly two thirds of patients. Among genuine toric candidates, up to a third had axis readings differing by an amount known to spoil correction. One device also nominated fewer candidates. The authors advise confirming measurements before committing a lens.
plos-pone-0357295:
Krzysztof Wilczyński led a team of eight authors linking blood molecules to thinking in older patients, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Tiny RNA molecules called microRNAs circulate in blood and regulate genes. The team ran a cross-sectional pilot study in a mixed inpatient and outpatient geriatric cohort, relating individual microRNAs to continuous measures of cognitive performance.

Wilczyński's RNA signatures could one day become simple blood tests for cognitive decline. Blood tests beat brain scans on cost and access, if the signals prove reliable. Pilot studies are small by design; their job is to find which molecules deserve larger trials. Cognitive decline is a growing burden as populations age, so even early leads toward cheap detection draw serious interest from clinicians and families alike.
plos-pone-0357395:
Moushumi Rani Dey and three colleagues published a pain study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They looked at how cold triggers pain signals in a cluster of nerve cells that serves the body, called the dorsal root ganglion. A sodium channel named Nav1.8, found in pain-sensing nerves, stood at the center of their work.

Dey's team showed that this channel helps control calcium signals inside the nerve cells when cold pain strikes. Calcium shifts are part of how a nerve cell fires and passes the pain message on. Pinning down the channel's role gives drug makers a concrete target: a drug that calms Nav1.8 might ease cold-triggered pain without dulling all feeling.
plos-pone-0357495:
Maria A. C. Wester Trejo and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE reviewing a decade of ANCA testing at a large Dutch teaching hospital. These antibody tests help diagnose autoimmune diseases that inflame blood vessels, but the standard testing order was set in specialist centers where the disease is common. In ordinary hospitals most positives may be false alarms, so the team re-examined over five thousand tested patients.

Only about one patient in twenty tested positive, and nearly two-thirds of those positives had no vasculitis at all; other autoimmune diseases, cancers, infections, or drugs explained many. Both tests ruled disease out well when negative, but starting with the antibody-specific test gave cleaner positives, and a second test sharpened accuracy. A second test is also recommended when a positive clashes with clinical doubt. The tailored strategy aims to cut false positives where the disease is rare.
plos-pone-0357595:
Sushma Swaroopa and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a fungus that lives inside the bark of a medicinal tree and may yield protective chemistry. Such fungi are rich sources of bioactive compounds. The team profiled the fungus's extract with advanced liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry, tested its ability to neutralize free radicals in a dish. They also modeled its main compound against a key antioxidant enzyme, and dosed mice before exposing them to gamma radiation.

One metabolite dominated the extract. Radical scavenging was real but moderate, clearly weaker than vitamin C in the same test. Computer modeling showed the main compound can sit against the protective enzyme superoxide dismutase, and in mice the extract more than doubled that enzyme's liver activity versus irradiated animals given nothing. This is early evidence of antioxidant potential worth purifying and testing further, not yet a proven radiation protectant.
plos-pone-0357795:
Jie Li and Xiaohong Wang published a 2026 control theory paper in PLOS ONE on keeping a special kind of neural network stable while it communicates over a cramped channel. These networks process complex-valued signals with time delays, and can only send sampled, compressed updates in bursts, resting between to save bandwidth. The authors design such an intermittent, quantized transmission scheme and prove mathematically when it still guarantees that the network settles exponentially fast.

Their two criteria, as solvable matrix inequalities, give the first explicit trade-off between transmission burst length and allowable rest fraction. A search procedure finds either limit once the other is chosen. Simulations on a small example network confirmed the scheme stabilizes the system while using far fewer transmissions. That quantitative link between rest time and switching wear, they argue, is what designers of networked controllers need.
plos-pone-0358195:
Qin Tong and Jun Liang studied glass-ceramics for nuclear waste in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Nuclear waste must stay locked away for thousands of years. One approach melts it into glass-ceramic material based on basalt. The pair used lanthanum, cerium, and neodymium as safe stand-ins for actinides, the radioactive elements in real waste.

Tong and Liang examined the material's structure and tested how fast the stand-in elements leach out in water. Slow leaching is the whole point: the waste form must hold its load even if groundwater reaches it. Results like these guide the design of waste forms long before any real actinides are used, keeping early testing safe and cheap.
plos-pone-0358595:
Niko Kargas leads a team of eight interviewing British military families who raise neurodivergent children, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Twelve parents described a support landscape split across health, education, welfare, and informal help, all inside a life of postings and deployments. The study asked how families find support, keep it, and what the effort costs them.

Support felt less like an entitlement than a prize repeatedly rewon. Each relocation broke clinical assessments, school arrangements, and diagnostic queues, and parents became the couriers of their own children's files, rebuilding trust with new professionals every move. Welfare services and informal networks genuinely helped, but access hinged on local knowledge and individual champions. The advocacy burden fell unevenly, often on mothers, and deployments reshuffled care at home. Families voiced pride and solidarity too, and resisted being praised as resilient when systems were the problem.
plos-pone-0358795:
Mohammad Mahboob Hussain Khan leads a team of eight authors in a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting thunderstorms in Bangladesh. Storms there threaten lives, crops, and buildings, above all in the northeast. The authors build separate forecast models for three high risk weather stations, Sylhet, Sreemangal, and Mymensingh, using four decades of monthly records.

They test thirty-six approaches, from classic time series statistics to neural networks, with and without climate inputs such as cloud cover, pressure, temperature, and rain. Removing the seasonal pattern first helped a great deal, and tree based models came out best at each station. Cloud cover proved the strongest single clue. Station level forecasts like these could give farmers and local officials earlier, more useful warnings.
plos-pone-0359395:
Siavash Shirzadeh Barough and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article using laboratory rats. It studies early life stress and its later effects on the offspring. Adolescent male rat pups whose early life was stressful showed impaired glucose control, anxiety-like behavior, and oxidative stress.

Against those harms the authors test saffron extract, from the spice crocus, for a protective effect. Animal work like this explores how hardship at the very start of life programs later health, and whether a natural compound can soften that programming. The findings feed the wider search for ways to shield children exposed to early adversity.
plos-pone-0360395:

Low energy availability means an athlete takes in too little food energy for her training load, which can harm health and performance. Screening-based studies show how widespread the risk is in a squad or sport. Coaches, team doctors, and sports dietitians use such figures to decide when routine screening should become standard in women's volleyball.

Teschendorff, Marabita, Lechner, and co-authors present a fixing method for Illumina methylation beadchip data. The Infinium chip was a leading tool for genome-wide association studies of these marks, which scan methylation across many people. A flaw is that its probes come in two different designs.

The two probe types give widely different data distributions, biasing results if left uncorrected. Their beta-mixture quantile method corrects that design bias. Better correction means reported links between methylation and disease are more likely real, an essential step as such studies inform medicine.  Large consortium studies adopted the correction as part of their standard pipelines.
pmc-4489295:
Metsalu and Vilo built ClustVis, described in 2015, a web tool for viewing clustered data. Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a widely used way to shrink high-dimensional data down to a plottable form. Users often follow it with a plot of two components, yet no easy web interface existed for the method.

ClustVis pairs PCA plots with heatmaps, which show clustered values as colored grids. Scientists can upload a data table and get publication-ready views without installing software. Clustering reveals groups in data from gene studies, surveys, and many other fields. A simple, shared tool helps teams check patterns before deeper analysis.
pmc-4532895:
Agarwal, Bell, Nam, and their colleagues studied microRNA target prediction in 2015. MicroRNAs guide gene silencing by pairing with sites on messenger RNAs. Pairing often involves the microRNA's seed region, but not all such canonical sites work equally well.

The authors combined computing with in vivo crosslinking data to learn what makes a site effective. Many messenger RNAs are targeted, yet context around the site shapes the outcome. Their model predicts which sites in mammalian messages truly repress a gene. Sharper predictions save lab effort and improve maps of how microRNAs control development and disease.
pmc-6027495:
M Danaei and colleagues reviewed how particle size affects lipid nanocarriers in medicine in 2018. Fat-based carriers can hold both water-loving and fat-loving drugs. They protect drugs from breakdown and raise the share that reaches the body.

Size and size spread strongly shape where carriers go and how long they last. Small, uniform particles tend to behave in a more predictable way in blood and tissue. The review gathers evidence on making and measuring particles to hit a target size. Formulators use it to set quality limits before a carrier is tested in people.
pmc-7003895:
Iris Nagtegaal, Robert Odze, David Klimstra, and coauthors presented the 2019 WHO classification of digestive tumors in 2019. The World Health Organization tumor classifications set the shared language of cancer diagnosis. Pathologists worldwide grade and name tumors by these books.

The digestive volume updates types for the esophagus, stomach, bowel, liver, and pancreas. Molecular findings now sit beside microscope appearance in several definitions. Some tumor groups were split or merged to match new evidence. Any lab diagnosing gut cancers works from this standard, which makes the summary widely consulted. The classification is revised on a regular cycle as new tumor evidence accumulates.
pmc-8728295:
Yasset Perez-Riverol and colleagues described in 2022 the PRIDE database, the world's largest public archive of proteomics data from mass spectrometry. PRIDE stores the raw evidence behind studies that identify and measure proteins in samples. It is also a founding member of the ProteomeXchange consortium, which coordinates protein data sharing worldwide.

The article reports the archive's growth and its newer services, including better search and links to other resources. It explains how researchers deposit data and how others reuse it to check findings or ask new questions. Open archives like PRIDE underpin the credibility of proteomics, since claims about proteins can be traced back to shared raw data.
pmc-8758495:
Harald Hampel, John Hardy, Kaj Blennow, and colleagues reviewed in 2021 the amyloid-beta pathway, now placed at the center of Alzheimer's disease research. Amyloid-beta is a small protein fragment that gathers into plaques in the brains of patients. Advances in molecular medicine have tied this pathway to the chain of events that leads to failing synapses, dying neurons, and dementia.

The authors lay out what is known about how amyloid-beta is produced, how it spreads, and how it injures the brain over time. They also discuss the pathway's place beside other suspects, such as tau protein. The review frames the debate behind the newest Alzheimer's drugs, which aim squarely at this pathway.
pmc-8960395:
Marco Solmi and a large team of collaborators pooled in 2021 the world's evidence on the age at which mental disorders first appear. Prevention and early treatment work best when services know when each disorder typically begins, yet the peak ages of onset were not firmly established. The team carried out a large scale meta-analysis of nearly two hundred epidemiological studies from many countries.

Combining those studies, they estimate the ages by which set shares of cases of each disorder have begun, from phobias and anxiety in childhood to later onset conditions. Their findings underline how many disorders start in the teenage years. The results give schools, clinics, and policymakers a factual basis for aiming early help at the right ages.
reflections-and-comments-1865-1895: Edwin Lawrence Godkin, the great editor of The Nation, reflects on thirty years of American life — politics, society, and morals. His high-minded, often sharp comments shaped liberal thought. The essential Godkin, in his own words. Reconstruction, reform, and the Gilded Age all feel his searching criticism.
remote-viewing-evaluation-air-1995:
The CIA paid for a hard count of remote viewing's worth, and the count ended the program in 1995. An Evaluation of Remote Viewing, by the American Institutes for Research and dated September 29, weighs the STAR GATE work in full. Two camps of reviewers split on the lab proof, but the field word was grim.

The study found the viewing of no use to spy work as it was run, whatever the lab numbers said. On its word the files were freed and the program shut that year. The report is the scientific epitaph of the psychic spy age. It closes twenty years of sealed work in one dry volume.
remy-daemonolatreiae-latin-1595:
Nicolas Rémy, a judge in Lorraine, published his Daemonolatreiae, three books on demon worship, in 1595. The Latin work draws on his own courtroom record. Rémy boasted of some nine hundred capital trials for witchcraft, a figure that makes his book the most prosecution-grounded demonology ever written.

He describes the sabbath, the pact, and the marks of witches from testimony he himself heard. His certainty never wavers across three books. The hunt is here described by its hunter, in learned Latin. Modern readers find the pride in the death toll hard to forget. No source shows the persecuting mind more completely from inside.
remy-demonolatry-1595:
Nicholas Remy was a French judge who sent scores of witches to their deaths. His Demonolatry dates from 1595. E. A. Ashwin turned it into English, and Montague Summers put that dress out in 1930. Remy drew on the trials of nine hundred folk in Lorraine.

Pacts, sabbats, and flights by night fill his dark scheme. Remy tells how to test, try, and burn those held for the craft. He writes with the calm of a man of law at his desk. The book is a chief text of the witch hunt mind of its age.
rontgen-neue-art-strahlen-1895:
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, a German physics professor, announced a strange new ray in late 1895. His short paper, On a New Kind of Rays, is given here in the German original. Within weeks, the news had circled the world.

Röntgen tells how the rays pass through wood, paper, and flesh, but not through bone or lead. He prints the now famous image of his wife's hand, bones and ring clear inside. Doctors grasped the use at once, and X-rays changed medicine forever. Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in physics for the find.
round-feudal-england-1895:
J. H. Round published Feudal England in 1895, a set of historical studies in medieval records. Round attacks the romantic picture of feudalism taught by Freeman and others. With charters, pipe rolls, and Domesday evidence, he shows Norman feudalism as a system imposed from above. Knight service and land tenure are recalculated with care.

Round's tone is combative, and his corrections stung his rivals. Later scholars confirmed much of his source criticism. The book marks a triumph of hard evidence over fine writing in medieval history. Round changed how England's feudal past could be studied. Specialists still cite his findings. General readers gain a bracing lesson in how history gets corrected.
sigwart-logic-vol1-1895:
Christoph Sigwart issued his Logik in German between 1873 and 1878, and Helen Dendy translated the first volume in 1895. Sigwart was a leading German logician of his century. Volume one centers on judgment, the act by which a mind joins or parts ideas and claims truth.

Sigwart builds his account from how thought works in real minds, not from bare form alone. He treats concepts, judgments, and the rules that guide sound thinking. Later logicians, among them the circle around Gottlob Frege, worked in a field his books helped shape. The volume gives English readers the core of his system. It rewards slow, close reading.
sigwart-logic-vol2-1895:
Helen Dendy's 1895 translation continues Christoph Sigwart's Logik with its second volume. The first volume dealt with judgment and the basic forms of thought. Volume two turns to method, the ordered paths by which inquiry moves toward truth.

Sigwart treats the logic of the sciences, showing how each field tests claims in its own way. He covers proof, error, and the steps that turn raw facts into firm knowledge. His aim is practical: to state how careful thinkers should proceed. Read with volume one, the book completes a major German system of logic. It shows nineteenth century rigor at full stretch.
smith-essays-philosophical-subjects-1795:
Adam Smith's Essays on Philosophical Subjects came out in 1795, five years after his death. Friends published the pieces he had kept back during his life. His History of Astronomy leads the set, tracing how minds explain the heavens. The Theory of the External Senses treats how we perceive the world outside us.

The essays show the philosopher behind the economist of the Wealth of Nations. Wonder, surprise, and the urge for system drive his account of science itself. Hume and others praised the astronomy essay in its day. Readers gain a Smith of curiosity and style, not ledgers alone. The posthumous volume rounds out his mind.
spr-proceedings-vol11-1895:
Volume eleven of the Proceedings, dated 1895, binds parts twenty seven through twenty nine. The SPR's journal of record moves into the mid 1890s with its habits fixed. Census results on hallucinations feed debate through these parts. Thought transference trials persist, run by younger members with new designs.

Piper's trance sittings still command the longest reports and the hardest questions. Other mediums, and cases of apparitions at death beds, fill out the record. The society prints dissent from its own ranks without flinching. Volume eleven shows the evidential debate settling into routine rigor. Its pages preserve names and cases later books all cite. Primary evidence, again, is the point.
stanton-womans-bible-vol-1-1895:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton published The Woman's Bible, Part 1 in 1895. Stanton, by then the elder leader of the suffrage movement, led a committee of women who commented on Bible passages about women. Part 1 covers the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.

The commentary challenges readings that used scripture to keep women subject, arguing that degrading passages reflect their writers, not God. Stanton's group read Genesis, Exodus, and the law codes with open skepticism and some humor. Suffrage groups feared the book would hurt the cause, and many disowned it. It became the founding text of feminist biblical criticism, a field that grew large in the next century.
subba-row-esoteric-writings-1895:
T. Subba Row left a small but weighty shelf of work, and A Collection of Esoteric Writings, out in 1895, saves it. Subba Row was a keen mind of India in the first crop of the new creed. He died young. His tracts gloss hard points of creed with the lore of his own land's old faith.

He oft set Blavatsky's claims in a more strict light. Fans prized his calm, sharp voice in rows of the day. The set is the chief mark of the creed's best mind from India. It bridges two worlds of thought. He left the creed's ranks while still a young man of gifts. His brief life makes this set a sad glimpse of what might have grown.
tarikh-i-rashidi-elias-ross-1895:
Mirza Muhammad Haidar wrote the Tarikh-i-Rashidi, a history of Central Asia's Moghuls. N. Elias and E. Denison Ross put the work into English in 1895. Haidar was Babur's cousin, and he rode with the men he describes.

The Chagatai khans and their wars fill his bold, personal chronicle. Family lines, raids, and lost kingdoms crowd the steppe and the oases. Haidar mixes memoir with history, and both gain life from the blend. The Mughal empire's Central Asian roots stand clear in his pages. Few chronicles of the region match its mix of action and witness.
tob-0095:
A London pamphlet of 1619 tells the case of Margaret and Phillippa Flower, servants at Belvoir Castle accused of killing the Earl of Rutland's young sons by witchcraft. Their mother Joan was also accused. The Wonderful Discoverie prints the charges, examinations, and confessions as Jacobean readers craved them.

Joan Flower died on the road to prison; her daughters were hanged at Lincoln. The pamphlet mixes court record with wonder and horror in equal measure. True-crime writing of the witch craze seldom gets closer to a real case. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10395:
Arthur Edward Waite surveyed the grimoire tradition in The Book of Ceremonial Magic, first published in 1898 and later revised. Waite knew the occult world from inside and wrote as both scholar and critic. He gathered rites that had passed hand to hand for centuries.

He prints and judges material from the Key of Solomon, the Grimorium Verum, and the Faust books, among others. Waite often doubts the value of black magic rites while still giving them in full. The result works as both a handbook of old rituals and a history of how magicians claimed to call spirits.
tob-10495:
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy reaches its middle panel in Purgatorio, presented in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1867 translation. Dante the poet climbs the mountain of Purgatory, guided for much of the way by Virgil. Souls there are not damned; they are being cleansed, and every step climbs toward Paradise.

Terrace by terrace, the seven deadly sins are purged, from pride at the bottom to lust at the top, with hymns, meetings, and stories at each level. Hope, not horror, is the ruling note, unlike the Inferno before it. Longfellow's version keeps Dante's movement in stately American English that generations of readers learned from.
tob-10795:
Monier Monier-Williams, Oxford's great Sanskritist, explained Buddhism in Buddhism in Connexion with Brahmanism and Hinduism by showing what it kept and what it rejected from the traditions around it. Buddhism did not appear in a vacuum. It argued with the ritual, caste, and sacrifice of its homeland.

Chapter by chapter, Monier-Williams sets Buddhist teaching beside Brahmanical practice: the gods, the soul, karma, and release all come under the Buddha's scrutiny. His map is careful, scholarly, and Victorian in framing. Readers get a systematic comparison that clarifies both sides, best used alongside Buddhist texts themselves, several of which stand nearby in this library.
tob-4295:
Sir John Woodroffe, a British judge in Calcutta, unveiled Tantra to Western readers under the name Arthur Avalon. His Principles of Tantra renders the Tantratattva, a Sanskrit digest of Tantric teaching, into English. Ritual, mantra, and the worship of Shakti, the goddess as power, form its core.

Woodroffe defends Tantra against missionary and scholarly contempt, presenting it as a serious path of worship and knowledge. His work began the modern study of the subject. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Avalon's pioneering exposition still marks the point where the West began to listen.
treaty-of-greenville-1795:
General Anthony Wayne signed the Treaty of Greenville in 1795 with the Native confederacy of the Old Northwest. The year before, Wayne's army had beaten the confederacy at the Battle of Fallen Timbers. Leaders of the Wyandot, Delaware, Shawnee, Miami, and other tribes came to Greenville to make peace on American terms.

The treaty drew a boundary line across the region and gave most of present-day Ohio to the United States. In return, the tribes received goods and yearly payments, and kept land west of the line on paper. White settlement poured into Ohio afterward, and the confederacy's power in the region was broken for good.
un-ga-res-195:
Korea's claim to one free state came back to the General Assembly in Resolution 195, adopted in December 1948. The UN Temporary Commission on Korea had reported on its work. The goals of the 1947 vote, the text admits, had not been met in full. Chief among the misses: Korea had not been made one. The fault lay in blocks the commission had met on the ground.

The Assembly backs the commission's findings. It declares that a lawful state now stands: the Government of the Republic of Korea. That state holds real rule over the part of Korea the commission could reach and watch. Most of the Korean people live there. Its rule rests on votes that were a true voice of the people, the text holds.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 195 (III), adopted on 12 December 1948, dealt with Korea one year after the Assembly's plan for free elections across the whole country. The Temporary Commission had been able to watch voting only in the south. The Assembly declared the Government of the Republic of Korea formed there to be lawful. It declared it based on a free vote, and the only such government in Korea.

The text called on the occupying powers to pull their forces out as soon as they could. It replaced the Temporary Commission with a seven-state Commission on Korea. The new commission was charged with helping to unite the country and easing the split's effects. It was also charged with watching the withdrawal.
un-sc-res-1295:
In a vote on 18 April 2000, the Council passed Resolution 1295 on Angola. UNITA rebels kept defying the peace deals they had signed. Sanctions on their arms, fuel, diamonds, funds, and travel were widely broken. An expert panel had traced how weapons and mercenaries still reached them.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets up a monitoring team of up to five experts for six months. The team will chase leads on sanctions breaches and report by 18 October 2000. States must demand end-use papers for arms exports and police their brokers. Diamond markets should punish trade in banned rough stones. The Council will decide by 18 November 2000 what to do about states found breaking the measures.
un-sc-res-1395:
Members of the Council unanimously adopted Resolution 1395 on Liberia on 27 February 2002. Sanctions imposed in 2001 charged Liberia with backing rebels in Sierra Leone. An expert panel had reported on Monrovia's conduct that October. A six-month review of the measures was due by May.

The Council brings the expert panel back for five weeks, starting no later than 11 March 2002. Up to five experts will visit Liberia and its neighbours. They will audit whether the government met the Council's demands. They will also log any breach of the arms, diamond, and travel measures. Their report is due by 8 April 2002, ahead of the sanctions review.
un-sc-res-1495:
A new peace plan for Western Sahara reached the Council in the summer of 2003. On 31 July 2003 the Council gave the plan its strong support. The Secretary-General's envoy had drafted it after years of deadlock. The Council said a political solution was now critically needed. Delay kept causing suffering and held back the whole Maghreb region.

The plan aimed at self-determination for the people of Western Sahara. The Council called on the parties to work with the United Nations toward accepting it. It asked states in the region to cooperate as well. It praised both sides for holding the ceasefire. MINURSO, the referendum mission, stayed in place to support the process.
un-sc-res-1595:
Resolution 1595 created an international investigation into the killing of Lebanon's former prime minister, Rafic Hariri. Hariri died in a huge Beirut car bombing in February 2005 that also killed 22 others. Lebanon asked for outside help, and the Council set up an independent commission that April.

The commission could question witnesses, gather evidence in Lebanon, and report its findings to the Council. Its work fed the later special tribunal for the case and raised pressure on Syria, whose troops left Lebanon that spring. The text is the founding record of one of the UN's most sensitive murder inquiries.
un-sc-res-1695:
North Korea test-fired a volley of ballistic missiles on 5 July 2006. Ten days later, on 15 July 2006, the Security Council condemned the launches. It voiced grave concern at the risk to peace in northeast Asia. Missiles of that kind can carry nuclear, chemical, or biological warheads. The Council recalled its standing rules against weapons proliferation.

It demanded that North Korea suspend all ballistic missile work. Pyongyang had to restore its earlier pledge to stop missile launches. All states had to guard against missile goods reaching North Korea. They also had to block purchases of such goods from it. The text set the stage for harsher sanctions after the nuclear test that followed.
un-sc-res-1795: Resolution 1795, from 2008, is a formal Security Council decision preserved in this collection in official-record wording. English Wikisource supplied the transcription. The act adds one more entry to the Council's running account of its work on peace and security. The account is kept here in the Council's own words rather than anyone's summary.
un-sc-res-1895: Under the number 1895, the Security Council filed a formal decision, and this collection holds the record text via Wikisource. The act's two halves work together: the preamble persuades, the operative part performs. Scholars and officials read them together to know what was decided and why, and the entry preserves them together for exactly that use.
un-sc-res-1995:
The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, nearing closure, is the subject of Resolution 1995 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 7 July 2011. The tribunal had to finish its work by the end of 2014. A residual body would take over its remaining tasks from July 2012. Staff losses threatened the timetable.

The text lets temporary judges stand for election as the tribunal's president or vice-president. A judge so elected holds the same powers as a permanent judge, with no change in status or pay. One named judge may work part time as a rare exception, and not as a model for others. States are urged again to hunt down the top fugitives still at large.
un-sc-res-295:
Guinea's safety brought a fact-finding mission from the Security Council on 3 August 1971. Guinea's permanent representative had written to the Council's president and addressed the Council in person. The complaint came months after a seaborne attack on Conakry that Guinea blamed on Portugal. The Council recalled that all member states must refrain from force against the territory or independence of any state.

The Council affirmed that Guinea's territorial integrity and political independence had to be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its own members to Guinea. The mission would consult the Guinean authorities and report on the situation at once. Its members would be named after talks between the Council's president and the Secretary-General. The question stayed on the Council's agenda. The move put Council members themselves on the ground to judge the threat Guinea faced.
un-sc-res-395: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 395, catalogued for 1949 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-95:
Egypt's Suez Canal restrictions on Israel-bound goods were ruled unlawful on 1 September 1951. The armistice between Israel and Egypt had run for nearly two and a half years. Egypt still stopped and searched ships in the Canal and barred goods meant for Israel. The truce chief of staff had pleaded with Egypt in June 1951 to end it, without success.

The Council found that Egypt's interference clashed with the peaceful settlement the armistice aimed at. With a permanent armistice in place, neither side could claim to be a belligerent. Egypt's searches were an abuse of any right of visit, search, and seizure. The Council called on Egypt to end the restrictions on shipping and goods through the Canal, wherever bound. Interference was to stop, apart from what safety in the Canal and the conventions in force required. Egypt did not comply, and the Canal question stayed live until 1956.
un-sc-res-995:
Western Sahara moved through the Council as Resolution 995, adopted unanimously on 26 May 1995. Work on naming who could vote in a self-rule referendum had picked up speed. Habits flagged by the Secretary-General were still slowing the settlement plan. The referendum mission's mandate was about to lapse.

The Council extends the mission, called MINURSO, only until 30 June 1995. It restates its pledge to hold the vote without more delay. Both parties must work with the mission in real cooperation. A team from the Council will travel to the region to speed things up. A longer renewal will turn on that team's report.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sanctions-busting for Angola's UNITA rebels is investigated under Resolution 1295, adopted on 18 April 2000. A Panel of Experts had reported widespread violations of the arms, petroleum, diamond, financial, and travel measures imposed on UNITA since 1993, including foreign military help and mercenaries. Illicit diamonds were UNITA's main funding source, and Angola's civil war was devastating civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council orders a monitoring mechanism of up to five experts for six months. It is to chase down violation leads, visit countries, and report to the Sanctions Committee by 18 October 2000. It sets 18 November 2000 as the deadline to decide on action against violating states and on tougher measures. It urges end-use controls on arms exports, SADC-led monitoring of fuel supplies near Angola's borders, and penalties in diamond markets for banned rough diamonds. It also urges a control system tracking diamonds from origin to market.

Liberia, not Western Sahara, is the subject of Resolution 1395. It was adopted unanimously on 27 February 2002. A year earlier, Resolution 1343 had placed sanctions on Liberia. The measures punished its government for backing rebels in Sierra Leone. An expert panel had reported on compliance in October 2001.

Members now brought that panel back for five more weeks. It would start no later than 11 March 2002. Up to five experts would visit Liberia and nearby states. They would audit whether the government obeyed the demands. They would also check for fresh violations of the sanctions. Their findings were due by 8 April 2002.

A peace plan for Western Sahara won the Council's strong backing in 2003. On 31 July, it adopted Resolution 1495. It acted under Chapter VI of the Charter. The Council stressed that a political fix was sorely needed. The stale dispute kept the territory's people in pain. It also threatened the wider region and blocked Maghreb growth.

The text backs the plan from the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy. It calls the plan the best political path, built on a deal between the two parties. Morocco and the Polisario Front must work with the UN toward taking it up. The plan promises the people's right to choose their own future. The release of all war prisoners is demanded once more.

The Beirut bombing that killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri gets an international investigation in this text of 7 April 2005. The 14 February 2005 attack killed Hariri and others and injured dozens. A United Nations fact-finding mission had reported troubling gaps in Lebanon's own inquiry and signs of a troubled security climate.

An International Independent Investigation Commission is set up to help Lebanon uncover the circumstances, causes, and consequences of the attack. The commission is to work with full access, and all states and parties are called on to cooperate with it completely. It had three months from becoming fully operational to finish its work.

Missiles over the Sea of Japan brought the Council together in 2006. On 15 July, it adopted Resolution 1695. North Korea had fired a volley of ballistic missiles days before. The launches broke its own pledge to pause such tests. No warning went to civil planes or ships in the area. Pyongyang also claimed to hold nuclear arms.

The text voices grave concern at the launches. It demands that North Korea halt its missile program. The old pause on launches must be restored as well. Member states must block missile-linked transfers to and from the North. Goods tied to mass-destruction arms are covered too. The text set the mold for the sanctions that followed the nuclear test that autumn.

The Ouagadougou political agreement of March 2007 was reached through direct talks between the Ivorian sides. It had restarted Côte d'Ivoire's peace process. On 15 January 2008 UNOCI and the French forces supporting it are renewed. A new prime minister drawn from the former rebels was in office under that deal.

Both mandates are renewed, and UNOCI is asked to support the agreement's key steps within its means: disarmament, voter identification, and preparations for elections. All parties are called on to protect women and children and to end abuses. The Secretary-General is to keep the Council closely informed, above all on the election timetable, which had already slipped and remained the central test of the peace deal.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union force, EUFOR, is renewed for twelve more months on 18 November 2009. As in prior years, full support is voiced for the High Representative and for the 1995 peace agreement. A March 2009 resolution had dealt with the High Representative's position and the international presence's future shape.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to maintain EUFOR as SFOR's legal successor, under unified command. The force keeps the main peace stabilization role for the military side of the peace agreement, working with the NATO headquarters presence under the arrangements the two organizations agreed in 2004. The parties are told again to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement.

Malawi's application for United Nations membership was approved for forwarding in Resolution 195, adopted unanimously on 9 October 1964. The Council had examined the request from the southeastern African country, which had become independent from Britain in July of that year under Hastings Banda. Like many new states of the period, it moved quickly to claim a UN seat.

The text recommends that the General Assembly admit Malawi to membership, and nothing more. That single step was legally essential, because the Assembly's vote on a new member is valid only after the Council recommends admission. The resolution is a neat marker of Malawi's first season as an independent state recognized by the wider world.

Housekeeping for the Rwanda tribunal fills Resolution 1995, adopted on 7 July 2011. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was due to close by 31 December 2014, handing over to the Residual Mechanism on 1 July 2012. Four permanent judges were set to move to the Appeals Chamber and two to leave. Staff retention was a stated worry, and fugitives were still at large.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council changes the tribunal's rules. Ad litem judges may be elected President and vote in that election. They hold the same powers as a permanent judge but no change in status or pay. One judge is allowed, as a one-off exception and no precedent, to work part-time from 1 September 2011 while holding another judicial post. The Council repeats its call for states to help bring the indictees to justice, and praises states that have taken in acquitted persons.

Resolution 295, adopted unanimously on 3 August 1971, sends a fact-finding team to Guinea. Guinea's ambassador had written to the Council's president, and its representative addressed the meeting, in a season when the small West African state feared attack from Portuguese-held territory next door. Guinea had already survived a seaborne invasion attempt the previous year.

The Council affirmed that Guinea's territorial integrity and political independence must be respected. It decided to send a special mission of three of its own members to Guinea, to consult the authorities and report on the situation immediately. The members were to be chosen after consultations between the Council president and the Secretary-General, and the matter stayed on the agenda.

Greece and Turkey, two neighbors that share the Aegean Sea, stood close to a clash in the summer of 1976. Their dispute covered the Aegean itself, including rights to explore its seabed. Tensions had risen to a dangerous level. The foreign ministers of both countries spoke to the Council. Resolution 395 was adopted by consensus on 25 August 1976.

The Council appealed to both governments to show the utmost restraint. They had to do all they could to lower tensions, so that talks could restart. Direct negotiations over their differences had to resume. Both sides were to work for solutions that each could accept. The Council also invited them to consider the help that courts could give. The International Court of Justice was pointed to in particular, for settling any legal differences the two sides identified.

Egypt's blockade of Israel-bound shipping through the Suez Canal is ruled against in Resolution 95, adopted on 1 September 1951 by eight votes to none with three abstentions. The truce supervision chief of staff had reported that Egypt kept interfering with goods passing through the canal for Israel, despite his direct plea in June to stop. Egypt's own delegate had promised cooperation at the 1949 Rhodes talks.

The Council found the practice an abuse of Egypt's rights and unjustified under the armistice, since a state of peace was supposed to be returning. It called on Egypt to end the restrictions on international commercial shipping through the canal, wherever it was bound. Egypt did not comply, and the canal stayed a flashpoint until 1956.

Western Sahara's promised independence vote kept slipping in 1995. Resolution 995, adopted unanimously on 26 May 1995, pressed for the referendum without more delay. Morocco and the Polisario Front had accepted a settlement plan years earlier. UN staff were identifying who could vote. Disputes over voter lists were slowing everything down.

MINURSO, the referendum mission, gained only a short extension, to 30 June 1995. Members praised progress in registering voters. They also voiced concern at practices blocking the plan. The Council decided to send its own mission to the region. A longer decision on MINURSO would wait for two reports, from the Secretary-General and from that visiting team.
uttaradhyayana-jacobi-1895: The Uttaradhyayana Sutra, a Jain canonical text translated by Jacobi in Sacred Books of the East volume 45. Its discourses teach nonviolence and renunciation. This edition preserves that Jain scripture. Those who study the era will use it.
verlaine-poems-1895:
Paul Verlaine was a French poet known for music and mood in verse. Gertrude Hall translated a selection of his poems into English in 1895. Verlaine led the Symbolist movement, which prized sound and suggestion. His life mixed fame, poverty, faith, and scandal.

The poems here move between soft love lyrics and sad songs of autumn and rain. Simple words carry deep feeling, and the lines seem to sing. Hall's versions helped bring Verlaine to English readers early. Readers who want the heart of French lyric poetry will find it here. The book is brief, tender, and easy to return to.
waddell-buddhism-of-tibet-1895:
L. Austine Waddell mapped Tibetan Buddhism for Western readers in The Buddhism of Tibet, or Lamaism, published in 1895. Waddell served as a medical officer with expeditions into the Himalayas and gathered much of his lore at first hand. Mystic cults, symbols, prayer wheels, masked dances, and demon lore fill his crowded, eager pages.

Victorian readers met here a faith they found both grand and strange, and scholars used the book for decades afterward. Waddell's judgments reflect his own age and creed, yet his store of observed detail stays valuable today. The work founded the Western study of Tibetan Buddhism, for better and worse, in one volume.
wells-time-machine-1895:
H. G. Wells wrote The Time Machine in 1895, his first great tale. A man of science builds a craft that rides through time. He tells his tale to a group of friends at a meal in Richmond. None of them quite trusts his wild claim.

The Time Traveller leaps to the year 802701 and finds mankind split in two. The soft Eloi live in ease on the ground, while the blind Morlocks toil in the dark below. He reads the split as the end of wealth and class drawn out to doom. The tale set the mold for all time trip tales since.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-6-189:
Volume six of Westcott's series presented the Chaldaean Oracles of Zoroaster in 1895. Percy Bullock wrote the introduction to the fragments. The translations came from Thomas Taylor and Isaac Preston Cory.

The Oracles are broken verses that guided Platonist philosophers of late antiquity. They teach about divine fire, the soul, and ritual ascent. Neoplatonists treated the sayings as scripture for their theurgy, or god-working. Westcott's edition became the Golden Dawn's working text of the Oracles. Its adepts actually ritualized passages that scholars only studied. Few small books of fragments have had larger occult influence than this one.
woodward-essay-toward-natural-history-ea:
John Woodward's Essay Toward a Natural History of the Earth appeared in 1695. Woodward, a London doctor and fossil collector, explains the Earth's crust by the Deluge. In the Flood's waters, he argues, the whole shell of the Earth dissolved. Matter then settled by weight as the waters fell.

Fossils are true remains of sea life, buried in that settling, on his account. His strata order matches the heaviness of their contents. The essay was the great contemporary answer to Burnet's Sacred Theory. Collectors across Europe corresponded with Woodward and sent him specimens. His museum later anchored Cambridge geology. The diluvial system here is stated at its strongest.
